Front propagation in hybrid reaction-diffusion epidemic models with spatial heterogeneity.
Part II: Pulsating traveling waves

Quentin Griette

Laboratoire de Mathématiques Appliquées du Havre, Université Le Havre Normandie,
EA 3821, FR CNRS 3335
25, rue Philippe Lebon, 76600 Le Havre, France
quentin.griette@univ-lehavre.fr

Hiroshi Matano

Meiji Institute for Advanced Study of Mathematical Sciences, Meiji University,
4-21-1 Nakano, Tokyo 164-8525, Japan
matano@meiji.ac.jp

August 24, 2026

Abstract

We consider a two-species reaction-diffusion system in one space dimension that is derived from an epidemiological model in a spatially periodic environment with two types of pathogens: the wild type and the mutant. The system is of a hybrid nature, partly cooperative and partly competitive, but neither of these entirely. As a result, the comparison principle does not hold. In the previous work, we studied the propagation properties of the solutions to the Cauchy problem for this system and showed, among other things, that the spreading speeds of the fronts to the right and to the left directions, denoted by cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L}, can be characterized by using certain principal eigenvalues, and studied the homogenization limit as the spatial period LL tends to 00, and also discussed the long-time behavior of solutions behind the fronts.

In the present paper we prove the existence of pulsating traveling waves in the right direction (resp. left direction) with speed cc for any c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} (resp. c≥cL∗c\geq c^{*}_{L}), where cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L} denote the aforementioned spreading speeds in the right and left directions. We also prove that the leading edge of any traveling wave has the exponential decay rate that is anticipated from formal linear analysis, thus extending part of the results of Hamel 2008 to systems of equations. Finally, we present an example in which the two speeds cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L} are different. This is done by considering a multi-scale singular limit problem. This result highlights a marked difference between our system and scalar KPP type equations.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the following reaction-diffusion system:

{ut=(σ⁡(x)​ux)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u+v))​u+μv​(x)​v−μu​(x)​u,t>0,x∈ℝ,vt=(σ⁡(x)​vx)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u+v))​v+μu​(x)​u−μv​(x)​v,t>0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&u_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)u_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(u+v)\big)u+\mu_{v}(x)v-\mu_{u}(x)u,&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &v_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)v_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(u+v)\big)v+\mu_{u}(x)u-\mu_{v}(x)v,&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

Here u⁡(t,x)u(t,x), v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) stand for the density of a population of individuals living in a periodically heterogeneous environment, ru​(x)∈ℝr_{u}(x)\in\mathbb{R} and rv​(x)∈ℝr_{v}(x)\in\mathbb{R} represent the intrinsic growth rate (which are not necessarily positive), κu​(x)>0\kappa_{u}(x)>0 and κv​(x)>0\kappa_{v}(x)>0 represent the intensity of the competition, and μu​(x)>0\mu_{u}(x)>0, μv​(x)>0\mu_{v}(x)>0 denote the mutation rates between the two populations. We assume that these coefficients, including the diffusion coefficient σ⁡(x)\sigma(x), are all LL-periodic.

The above problem is motivated partly by the study of SIS epidemiological models describing the propagation of pathogens that are subject to mutations, such as the following:

{∂tSt=∂x(σ⁡(x)​∂xS)−(β1​(x)​I1+β2​(x)​I2)​S+γ1​(x)​I1+γ2​(x)​I2,t>0,x∈ℝ,∂tI1=∂x(σ⁡(x)​∂xI1)+β1​(x)​S​I1−γ1​(x)​I1+μ2​(x)​I2−μ1​(x)​I1,t>0,x∈ℝ,∂tI2=∂x(σ⁡(x)​∂xI2)+β2​(x)​S​I2−γ2​(x)​I2+μ1​(x)​I1−μ2​(x)​I2,t>0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}S_{t}=\partial_{x}(\sigma(x)\partial_{x}S)-\big(\beta_{1}(x)I_{1}+\beta_{2}(x)I_{2}\big)S+\gamma_{1}(x)I_{1}+\gamma_{2}(x)I_{2},&&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &\partial_{t}I_{1}=\partial_{x}(\sigma(x)\partial_{x}I_{1})+\beta_{1}(x)SI_{1}-\gamma_{1}(x)I_{1}+\mu_{2}(x)I_{2}-\mu_{1}(x)I_{1},&&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &\partial_{t}I_{2}=\partial_{x}(\sigma(x)\partial_{x}I_{2})+\beta_{2}(x)SI_{2}-\gamma_{2}(x)I_{2}+\mu_{1}(x)I_{1}-\mu_{2}(x)I_{2},&&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{aligned}\right. (1.2)

Here the β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} denote the infection rates, γ1,γ2\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2} the recovery rates, and μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2} stand for the mutation rates between the pathogens.

It is not difficult to show that the quantity N⁡(t,x):=S⁡(t,x)+I1​(t,x)+I2​(t,x)N(t,x):=S(t,x)+I_{1}(t,x)+I_{2}(t,x) satisfies a pure diffusion equation ∂tN=∂x(σ⁡(x)​∂xN)\partial_{t}N=\partial_{x}\left(\sigma(x)\partial_{x}N\right). Therefore, if we assume that N⁡(0,x)N(0,x) is constant in xx, then N⁡(t,x)N(t,x) remains constant in tt and xx. Thus we obtain that u=I1u=I_{1}, v=I2v=I_{2} satisfy (1.1) with r∗​(x):=N​βi​(x)−γi​(x)r_{*}(x):=N\beta_{i}(x)-\gamma_{i}(x) and κi​(x):=βi​(x)\kappa_{i}(x):=\beta_{i}(x), where i=1,2i=1,2 and ∗=u,v*=u,v . Hence the propagation dynamics of (1.2) is equivalent to that of (1.1).

System (1.2) describes the propagation of a genetically unstable pathogen in a population of hosts which exhibit heterogeneity in space. This heterogeneity represents the spatially heterogeneous environment that affects the behavior of individuals depending on where they are. Spatial heterogeneity in the use of antibiotics, fungicides or insecticides affects the transmission of pathogens and pests and is explored as a way to minimize the risk of emergence of drug resistance [7]. Beaumont et al [4] study a related model of propagation of salmonella in an industrial hen house. In their study the heterogeneity comes from the alignment of cages separated by free space that allow farmers to take care of the animals. Griette et al [13] studied the propagation properties of a closely related model in the context of the evolution of drug resistance.

The propagation speed of the solutions of reaction-diffusion equations is often linked to special solutions called traveling wave solutions, that are particular solutions that propagate at a prescribed speed. There exists a large literature on traveling wave solutions and the propagation dynamics of solutions to reaction-diffusion equations and systems, see [19, 8, 2, 3, 30, 22, 27, 20, 21] among others. When the coefficients depend periodically on the spatial variable such as (1.1), the traveling waves are often called pulsating traveling waves, see [26, 32, 5, 31] among others.

Our system has a rather intriguing character in the sense that it is cooperative when (u,v)(u,v) is small while the competitive nature becomes dominant when (u,v)(u,v) is large. Therefore the standard comparison principle does not apply to the entire system. Such a system has been studied by Wang [28], Wang and Castillo-Chavez [29], Griette and Raoul [16], Girardin [12, 11], and Morris, Börger and Crooks [23], when the coefficients are homogeneous in space. However, in our case, the coefficients are spatially periodic. As far as scalar equations are concerend, there is a large literature on equations with periodic coefficients, notably [26, 32, 5, 31, 21]. As for systems, Alfaro and Griette [1] constructed a traveling wave for a related system that travels at the expected minimal speed. The special case where the coefficients are spatially homogeneous has been treated in [28, 29, 16, 12, 11, 23],

In our previous work [15], we considered system (1.1) under the initial condition

u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),v⁡(0,x)=v0​(x),x∈ℝ,u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\ \ v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\quad\ x\in\mathbb{R}, (1.3)

where u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are bounded nonnegative functions on ℝ\mathbb{R} whose supports are, in most cases, localized in space. Among other things, we proved that the solutions fronts propagate to the right and to the left asymptotically at constant speeds, that can be computed from a family of linearized eigenproblems around the leading edge. We also studied the behavior of the solution far behind the propagation front and proved the convergence to the unique steady state in the case where the coefficients are spatially homogeneous or rapidly oscillating. Finally, we studied the homogenization problem as L→0L\to 0 and determined the effective coefficients of the homogenized limit.

In the present paper, we focus on traveling waves and study their existence and qualitative properties. We first prove the existence of pulsating traveling waves in the right (resp. left) direction for any speed c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} (resp. c≥cL∗c\geq c^{*}_{L}). We also show that the leading edge of any traveling wave decays exponentially as x→∞x\to\infty (or quasi-exponentially in the critical case where c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R} or c=cL∗c=c^{*}_{L}). This result implies that all the pulsating traveling waves fulfill the ansatz that is anticipated from formal linear analysis. This extends part of the results of Hamel [17] to systems of equations. We note that our existence proof for the critical case c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R} or c=cL∗c=c^{*}_{L} does not rely on the usual limiting argument c→cR∗,cL∗c\to c^{*}_{R},c^{*}_{L}. We instead give a direct proof of the existence for the critical case by constructing super- and sub-solutions that are different from the non-critical case c>cR∗,cL∗c>c^{*}_{R},c^{*}_{L}.

Next, we consider the case where the coefficients are spatially homogeneous or rapidly oscillating, and prove that the profile of the traveling wave far behind its front converges to the unique periodic (or homogeneous) steady state. Finally, we present an example where cR∗≠cL∗c^{*}_{R}\neq c^{*}_{L}. This is done by a multi-scale singular limit analysis. We remark that, in the scalar KPP equation, the left and right critical wave speeds are always equal, even if the coefficients are not symmetric in xx, which is a consequence of the Fredholm alternative. This last result highlights a marked difference between scalar equations and systems.

Our paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we first recall key mathematical notions such as principal eigenvalues of various kinds, left and right spreading speeds, and state their basic properties. This will be done in subsection 2.1. Then, in subsections 2.2 and 2.3, we present our main results including the existence of critical and non-critical traveling waves (Theorem 2.13), decay properties along the leading edge (Theorem 2.17), convergence to the steady states in the spatially homogeneous and rapidly oscillating cases (Theorem 2.20), and the construction of an example with asymmetric propagation speeds (Theorem 2.22). The proofs of Theorems 2.13, 2.17, 2.20 and 2.22 will be given in sections 3, 4, 5 and 6, respectively.

2 Main results

Throughout this article we make the following assumption on the coefficients of (1.1).

Assumption 1 (Cooperative-competitive system).

The coefficients σ⁡(x)>0\sigma(x)>0, κu​(x)>0\kappa_{u}(x)>0, κv​(x)>0\kappa_{v}(x)>0, μv​(x)>0\mu_{v}(x)>0, μu​(x)>0\mu_{u}(x)>0, are LL-periodic positive continuous functions and ru​(x)r_{u}(x), rv​(x)r_{v}(x) are LL-periodic continuous functions of arbitrary sign. We assume moreover that σ∈C1​(ℝ)\sigma\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}).

Remark 2.1.

In formulating our problem, we chose to use the same diffusion coefficient σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) for uu and vv, in order to make the connection between (1.1) and (1.2) clearer. However, most of the results in the present paper remain to hold even if the diffusion coefficients for uu and vv are different; in particular, the existence result for traveling waves (Theorem 2.13) and the result on the exponential decay (Theorem 2.17) can easily be extended to the case of unequal diffusion coefficients.

To facilitate the statement of our results, we introduce the following notations:

rmax:=supx∈ℝmax(ru(x),rv(x)),κmax:=supx∈ℝmax(κu(x),κv(x)),μmax:=supx∈ℝmax(μu(x),μv(x)),σmax:=supx∈ℝσ(x),rmin:=infx∈ℝmin(ru(x),rv(x)),κmin:=infx∈ℝmin(κu(x),κv(x)),μmin:=infx∈ℝmin(μu(x),μv(x)),σmin:=infx∈ℝσ(x),K¯:=rmaxκmin.\begin{gathered}r_{\max}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max\big(r_{u}(x),r_{v}(x)\big),\ \ \kappa_{\max}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max\big(\kappa_{u}(x),\kappa_{v}(x)\big),\\ \mu_{\max}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max\big(\mu_{u}(x),\mu_{v}(x)\big),\ \ \sigma_{\max}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\sigma(x),\\ r_{\min}:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\min\big(r_{u}(x),r_{v}(x)\big),\ \ \kappa_{\min}:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\min\big(\kappa_{u}(x),\kappa_{v}(x)\big),\\ \mu_{\min}:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\min\big(\mu_{u}(x),\mu_{v}(x)\big),\ \ \sigma_{\min}:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\sigma(x),\ \ \overline{K}:=\frac{r_{\max}}{\kappa_{\min}}.\end{gathered} (2.1)

Before presenting our main results in this section, we remark that nonnegative solutions of (1.1) are all bounded as t→+∞t\to+\infty.

Proposition 2.2 (Basic boundedness estimate [15, Proposition 4]).

Let (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) be a solution of (1.1) with nonnegative bounded initial data (u0​(x),v0​(x))(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)). Then u⁡(t,x)≥0u(t,x)\geq 0, v⁡(t,x)≥0v(t,x)\geq 0 for all t≥0,x∈ℝt\geq 0,x\in\mathbb{R}, and

u⁡(t,x)+v⁡(t,x)≤max⁡(K¯,supx∈ℝ(u0​(x)+v0​(x)))for allt≥0,x∈ℝ,u(t,x)+v(t,x)\leq\max\big(\overline{K},\,\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}(u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x))\big)\ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ t\geq 0,x\in\mathbb{R}, (2.2)
lim supt→+∞supx∈ℝ(u⁡(t,x)+v⁡(t,x))≤K¯.\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big(u(t,x)+v(t,x)\big)\leq\overline{K}. (2.3)

In particular, if u0​(x)+v0​(x)≤K¯​(x∈ℝ)u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x)\leq\overline{K}\,(x\in\mathbb{R}), then u⁡(t,x)+v⁡(t,x)≤K¯​(t≥0,x∈ℝ)u(t,x)+v(t,x)\leq\overline{K}\,(t\geq 0,\,x\in\mathbb{R}).

2.1 Principal eigenproblems and spreading speed

In this subsection we recall some of the notions and basic results presented in our previous paper [15]. They will be used in our later arguments.

The linearized system associated with (1.1) is the following.

{ut=(σ⁡(x)​ux)x+ru​(x)​u+μv​(x)​v−μu​(x)​u,t>0,x∈ℝ,vt=(σ⁡(x)​vx)x+rv​(x)​v+μu​(x)​u−μv​(x)​v,t>0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&u_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)u_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{u}(x)u+\mu_{v}(x)v-\mu_{u}(x)u,&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &v_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)v_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{v}(x)v+\mu_{u}(x)u-\mu_{v}(x)v,&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{aligned}\right. (2.4)

Note that this is a cooperative system. We first define the notions of periodic principal, λ\lambda-periodic principal and Dirichlet principal eigenelements as follows.

Definition 1 (Periodic principal eigenpair).

By a periodic principal eigenpair associated with (2.4) we mean any pair (λ1p​e​r,(φ⁡(x),ψ⁡(x)))\big(\lambda_{1}^{per},(\varphi(x),\psi(x))\big) where λ1p​e​r∈ℝ\lambda_{1}^{per}\in\mathbb{R}, φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) and ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) are positive LL-periodic smooth functions that satisfy

{L1​[φ,ψ]​(x):=(σ⁡(x)​φx)x+ru​(x)​φ+μv​(x)​ψ−μu​(x)​φ=λ1p​e​r​φ,L2​[φ,ψ]​(x):=(σ⁡(x)​ψx)x+rv​(x)​ψ+μu​(x)​φ−μv​(x)​ψ=λ1p​e​r​ψ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&L^{1}[\varphi,\psi](x):=\big(\sigma(x)\varphi_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{u}(x)\varphi+\mu_{v}(x)\psi-\mu_{u}(x)\varphi=\lambda_{1}^{per}\varphi,\\ &L^{2}[\varphi,\psi](x):=\big(\sigma(x)\psi_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{v}(x)\psi+\mu_{u}(x)\varphi-\mu_{v}(x)\psi=\lambda_{1}^{per}\psi.\end{aligned}\right. (2.5)

We call λ1p​e​r\lambda_{1}^{per} the periodic principal eigenvalue and (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) a principal eigenvector.

It follows from the Krein-Rutman Theorem that λ1p​e​r\lambda_{1}^{per} is unique, and that (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) is unique up to multiplication by a positive scalar.

Definition 2 (λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenpair).

For λ>0\lambda>0, by a λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenpair associated with (2.4) we mean any pair (k⁡(λ),(φ⁡(x),ψ⁡(x)))\big(k(\lambda),(\varphi(x),\psi(x))\big) where k⁡(λ)∈ℝk(\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}, φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) and ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) are positive LL-periodic smooth functions that satisfy

{Lλ1​[φ,ψ]​(x):=eλ​x​L1​[e−λ​x​φ,e−λ​x​ψ]​(x)=k⁡(λ)​φ,Lλ2​[φ,ψ]​(x):=eλ​x​L2​[e−λ​x​φ,e−λ​x​ψ]​(x)=k⁡(λ)​ψ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&L^{1}_{\lambda}[\varphi,\psi](x):=e^{\lambda x}L^{1}[e^{-\lambda x}\varphi,e^{-\lambda x}\psi](x)=k(\lambda)\varphi,\\ &L^{2}_{\lambda}[\varphi,\psi](x):=e^{\lambda x}L^{2}[e^{-\lambda x}\varphi,e^{-\lambda x}\psi](x)=k(\lambda)\psi.\end{aligned}\right. (2.6)

or, equivalently,

{(σ⁡(x)​φx)x−2​λ​σ​(x)​φx+(λ2​σ​(x)−λ​σx​(x)+ru​(x))​φ+μv​(x)​ψ−μu​(x)​φ=k⁡(λ)​φ,(σ⁡(x)​ψx)x−2​λ​σ​(x)​ψx+(λ2​σ​(x)−λ​σx​(x)+rv​(x))​ψ+μu​(x)​φ−μv​(x)​ψ=k⁡(λ)​ψ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&\big(\sigma(x)\varphi_{x}\big)_{x}-2\lambda\sigma(x)\varphi_{x}+\big(\lambda^{2}\sigma(x)-\lambda\sigma_{x}(x)+r_{u}(x)\big)\varphi+\mu_{v}(x)\psi-\mu_{u}(x)\varphi=k(\lambda)\varphi,\\ &\big(\sigma(x)\psi_{x}\big)_{x}-2\lambda\sigma(x)\psi_{x}+\big(\lambda^{2}\sigma(x)-\lambda\sigma_{x}(x)+r_{v}(x)\big)\psi+\mu_{u}(x)\varphi-\mu_{v}(x)\psi=k(\lambda)\psi.\end{aligned}\right. (2.6′)

We call k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) the λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenvalue and (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) a λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenvector.

Again by the Krein-Rutman Theorem, for each λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) is unique and that (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) is unique up to multiplication by a positive scalar. Clearly we have k⁡(0)=λ1p​e​rk(0)=\lambda_{1}^{per}.

Definition 3 (Dirichlet principal eigenpair).

Let R>0R>0 be given. By a Dirichlet principal eigenpair on (−R,R)(-R,R) associated with (2.4) we mean any pair (λ1R,(φ⁡(x),ψ⁡(x)))\big(\lambda_{1}^{R},(\varphi(x),\psi(x))\big) where λ1R∈ℝ\lambda_{1}^{R}\in\mathbb{R}, φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) and ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) are positive smooth functions on [−R,R][-R,R] that satisfy

{(σ⁡(x)​φx)x+ru​(x)​φ+μv​(x)​ψ−μu​(x)​φ=λ1R​φ,(σ⁡(x)​ψx)x+rv​(x)​ψ+μu​(x)​φ−μv​(x)​ψ=λ1R​ψ,\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&\big(\sigma(x)\varphi_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{u}(x)\varphi+\mu_{v}(x)\psi-\mu_{u}(x)\varphi=\lambda_{1}^{R}\varphi,\\ &\big(\sigma(x)\psi_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{v}(x)\psi+\mu_{u}(x)\varphi-\mu_{v}(x)\psi=\lambda_{1}^{R}\psi,\end{aligned}\right. (2.7a)
and
φ⁡(−R)=ψ⁡(−R)=0​ and ​φ​(R)=ψ⁡(R)=0.\varphi(-R)=\psi(-R)=0\text{ and }\varphi(R)=\psi(R)=0. (2.7b)

We call λ1R\lambda_{1}^{R} the principal eigenvalue and (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) a Dirichlet principal eigenvector.

As before, the Krein-Rutman theorem ensures that λ1R\lambda_{1}^{R} is unique and (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) is unique up to multiplication by a positive scalar.

    For each λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, there exists a λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenpair (k⁡(λ),(φ,ψ))\big(k(\lambda),(\varphi,\psi)\big) with φ⁡(x)>0\varphi(x)>0 and ψ⁡(x)>0\psi(x)>0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, which solves (2.6), and (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) is unique up to the multiplication by a positive scalar.

By (2.9), we see that k⁡(λ)>0k(\lambda)>0 for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} if rmin>0r_{\min}>0. However, as we do not assume sign conditions on the intrinsic growth rates ru,rvr_{u},r_{v} at this stage, k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) can possibly take negative values for some λ\lambda.

Proposition 2.5 (Comparison of the principal eigenvalues [15, Theorem 2.1]).

Let Assumption 1 hold true. Then the mapping R↦λ1RR\mapsto\lambda_{1}^{R} is strictly increasing, and λ1R<k⁡(λ)\lambda_{1}^{R}<k(\lambda) for all R>0R>0 and λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. Furthermore,

limR→+∞λ1R=minλ∈ℝ⁡k⁡(λ).\lim_{R\to+\infty}\lambda_{1}^{R}=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}k(\lambda). (2.10)

From (2.10) we see that

limR→+∞λ1R=minλ∈ℝ⁡k⁡(λ)≤k⁡(0)=λ1p​e​r,\lim_{R\to+\infty}\lambda_{1}^{R}=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}k(\lambda)\leq k(0)=\lambda_{1}^{per},

but the equality does not hold in general.

Under some symmetry conditions, k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) is an even function.

Proposition 2.6 ([15, Proposition 3]).

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds true, and assume further that either:

  1. (i)

    μu​(x)=μv​(x)\mu_{u}(x)=\mu_{v}(x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, or

  2. (ii)

    all coefficients are even: σ⁡(x)=σ⁡(−x)\sigma(x)=\sigma(-x), ru​(x)=ru​(−x)r_{u}(x)=r_{u}(-x), rv​(x)=rv​(−x)r_{v}(x)=r_{v}(-x), μu​(x)=μu​(−x)\mu_{u}(x)=\mu_{u}(-x) and rv​(x)=ru​(−x)r_{v}(x)=r_{u}(-x), for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}.

Then the function λ↦k⁡(λ)\lambda\mapsto k(\lambda) is even, i.e. k⁡(λ)=k⁡(−λ)k(\lambda)=k(-\lambda) for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. Consequently, we have

limR→+∞λ1R=minλ∈ℝ⁡k⁡(λ)=k⁡(0)=λ1p​e​r.\lim_{R\to+\infty}\lambda_{1}^{R}=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}k(\lambda)=k(0)=\lambda_{1}^{per}. (2.11)

We remark that k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) is always an even function in the case of scalar KPP type equations even if the coefficients are not even functions. This is a consequence of the Fredholm alternative.

Next we introduce the notion of front-like initial data.

Definition 4.

The pair of bounded nonnegative functions (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) on ℝ\mathbb{R} that appears in (1.3) is called right front-like if there exists a real number KK such that

lim infx→−∞min(u0(x),v0(x))>0,u0(x)=v0(x)=0for allx≥K.\liminf_{x\to-\infty}\min(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x))>0,\quad u_{0}(x)=v_{0}(x)=0\ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ x\geq K.

It is called left front-like if there exists a real number KK such that

u0​(x)=v0​(x)=0for allx≤K,lim infx→+∞min⁡(u0​(x),v0​(x))>0.u_{0}(x)=v_{0}(x)=0\ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ x\leq K,\quad\liminf_{x\to+\infty}\min(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x))>0.
Theorem 2.7 (Spreading speeds for front-like initial data [15, Theorem 2.2]).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and assume that λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. Then there exist real numbers cR∗c^{*}_{R}, cL∗c^{*}_{L} and a positive number η>0\eta>0 such that for any solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1)–(1.3) whose initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is right front-like, it holds that

{lim inft→∞[infx≤c​tmin(u(t,x),v(t,x))]≥η,for allc<cR∗,lim supt→∞[supx≥c​tmax(u(t,x),v(t,x))]=0,for allc>cR∗,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\ \liminf_{t\to\infty}\left[\inf_{x\leq ct}\min(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]\geq\eta,\ \ &\text{for all}\ \ c<c^{*}_{R},\\[9.0pt] \displaystyle\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\left[\sup_{x\geq ct}\max(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]=0,\ \ &\text{for all}\ \ c>c^{*}_{R},\end{cases} (2.12)

while for any solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1)–(1.3) whose initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) is left front-like, it holds that

{lim inft→∞[infx≥−c​tmin(u(t,x),v(t,x))]≥η,for allc<cL∗,lim supt→∞[supx≤−c​tmax(u(t,x),v(t,x))]=0,for allc>cL∗.\begin{cases}\displaystyle\ \liminf_{t\to\infty}\left[\inf_{x\geq-ct}\min(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]\geq\eta,\ \ &\text{for all}\ \ c<c^{*}_{L},\\[9.0pt] \displaystyle\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\left[\sup_{x\leq-ct}\max(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]=0,\ \ &\text{for all}\ \ c>c^{*}_{L}.\end{cases} (2.13)

Furthermore, we have the following formula:

cR∗=infλ>0k⁡(λ)λ=minλ>0⁡k⁡(λ)λcL∗=infλ<0k⁡(λ)−λ=minλ<0⁡k⁡(λ)−λ=minλ>0⁡k⁡(−λ)λ,c^{*}_{R}=\inf_{\lambda>0}\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}=\min_{\lambda>0}\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}\quad\ \ c^{*}_{L}=\inf_{\lambda<0}\frac{k(\lambda)}{-\lambda}=\min_{\lambda<0}\frac{k(\lambda)}{-\lambda}=\min_{\lambda>0}\dfrac{k(-\lambda)}{\lambda}, (2.14)

where k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) is the λ\lambda-principal periodic eigenvalue defined in Definition 2.

Remark 2.8.

The formula (2.14) can be regarded as the one-dimensional version of the Gärtner-Freidlin formula for scalar equations [10, 6]. Note that the constant η\eta in (2.12) and (2.13) does not depend on the choice of (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}).

Definition 5 (Right- and left spreading speeds).

The above quantities cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L} are called the right spreading speed and left spreading speed of solutions to (1.1), respectively.

Proposition 2.9 ([15, Proposition 5]).

Let σmin\sigma_{\min}, σmax\sigma_{\max}, rminr_{\min}, rmaxr_{\max} be the constants that appear in (2.1). Then

cR∗≤2​σmax​rmax,cL∗≤2​σmax​rmax.c^{*}_{R}\leq 2\sqrt{\sigma_{\max}r_{\max}},\quad c^{*}_{L}\leq 2\sqrt{\sigma_{\max}r_{\max}}.

Furthermore, if rmin>0r_{\min}>0, then

cR∗≥2​σmin​rmin,cL∗≥2​σmin​rmin.c^{*}_{R}\geq 2\sqrt{\sigma_{\min}r_{\min}},\quad c^{*}_{L}\geq 2\sqrt{\sigma_{\min}r_{\min}}.
Remark 2.10.

As mentioned in Remark 2.4, k⁡(λ)k(\lambda) can possibly take negative values if rmin<0r_{\min}<0, in which case cR∗c^{*}_{R} or cL∗c^{*}_{L} becomes negative. A negative speed implies that the front is retreating. If we assume λ⁡(0)(=λ1p​e​r)>0\lambda(0)(=\lambda_{1}^{per})>0 as in Theorem 2.7, then at least one of cR∗,cL∗c^{*}_{R},c^{*}_{L} is positive by the convexity of λ↦k⁡(λ)\lambda\mapsto k(\lambda).

If we assume that both cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L} are positive, then the following theorem holds.

Theorem 2.11 (Hair-trigger effect [15, Theorem 2.3]).

Let Assumption 1 hold true. Then the following three conditions are equivalent:

(a)​λ1R>0for some​R>0,(b)​minλ∈ℝ⁡k⁡(λ)>0,(c)​cR∗>0,cL∗>0.{\rm(a)}\ \lambda_{1}^{R}>0\ \ \hbox{for some}\ R>0,\quad\ {\rm(b)}\ \min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}k(\lambda)>0,\quad\ {\rm(c)}\ c^{*}_{R}>0,\ c^{*}_{L}>0.

If any of these conditions holds, there exists a number η>0\eta>0 depending only on the coefficients of system (1.1) such that for any nonnegative bounded initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) satisfying (u0​(x),v0​(x))≢(0,0)(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x))\not\equiv(0,0), the solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) of (1.1)–(1.3) has the following property:

lim inft→+∞u⁡(t,x)≥ηandlim inft→+∞v⁡(t,x)≥ηfor allx∈ℝ.\liminf_{t\to+\infty}u(t,x)\geq\eta\ \ \text{and}\ \ \liminf_{t\to+\infty}v(t,x)\geq\eta\ \ \text{for all}\ \ x\in\mathbb{R}. (2.15)

Furthermore, if, in addition, u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are compactly supported, then the right front and the left front of (u,v)(u,v) propagate at the speed cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L}, respectively. More precisely,

lim inft→∞[inf0≤x≤c​tmin⁡(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))]≥η,for all​ 0<c<cR∗,\displaystyle\displaystyle\ \liminf_{t\to\infty}\left[\inf_{0\leq x\leq ct}\min(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]\geq\eta,\ \ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ 0<c<c^{*}_{R}, (2.16a)
lim supt→∞[supx≥c​tmax⁡(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))]=0,for allc>cR∗.\displaystyle\displaystyle\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\left[\sup_{x\geq ct}\max(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]=0,\ \ \ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*}_{R}. (2.16b)
lim inft→∞[inf−c​t≤x≤0min⁡(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))]≥η,for all​ 0<c<cL∗,\displaystyle\displaystyle\ \liminf_{t\to\infty}\left[\inf_{-ct\leq x\leq 0}\min(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]\geq\eta,\ \ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ 0<c<c^{*}_{L}, (2.17a)
lim supt→∞[supx≤−c​tmax⁡(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))]=0,for allc>cL∗.\displaystyle\displaystyle\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}\left[\sup_{x\leq-ct}\max(u(t,x),v(t,x))\right]=0,\ \ \ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*}_{L}. (2.17b)

The assertions (2.16a) and (2.17a) hold for any nonnegative nontrivial solution of (1.1).

Proposition 2.12 ([15, Proposition 6]).

Let the assumption (i) or (ii) of Proposition 2.6 hold, along with the condition λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. Then cR∗=cL∗>0c^{*}_{R}=c^{*}_{L}>0. In particular, if all the coefficients are spatially homogeneous, then cR∗=cL∗>0c^{*}_{R}=c^{*}_{L}>0.

2.2 Traveling waves

Now we are ready to state the main results of the present paper. Throughout the rest of this section, we assume, as in Theorem 2.7, that λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. This condition implies that (u,v)=(0,0)(u,v)=(0,0) is unstable under positive LL-periodic perturbations. Without this condition, any solution of (1.1) with small nonnegative initial data decays to 00 as t→∞t\to\infty uniformly on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

First we recall the notion of traveling wave solutions under a spatially periodic environment. We distinguish the “right traveling waves” and “left traveling waves”.

Definition 6 (Traveling wave solutions).

Let c>0c>0 be given and (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) be an entire solution to (1.1), i.e. a solution that is defined for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. We say that (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) is a right traveling wave propagating at speed cc if it satisfies

u(t+Lc,x)=u(t,x−L),v(t+Lc,x)=v(t,x−L),for all(t,x)∈ℝ2,u\left(t+\frac{L}{c},x\right)=u(t,x-L),\;v\left(t+\frac{L}{c},x\right)=v(t,x-L),\ \ \text{for all}\ \ (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, (2.18)

as well as the following asymptotics at x=±∞x=\pm\infty:

limx→+∞u(t,x)=0,limx→+∞v(t,x)=0,for allt∈ℝ,\displaystyle\lim_{x\to+\infty}u(t,x)=0,\;\lim_{x\to+\infty}v(t,x)=0,\ \ \text{for all}\ \ t\in\mathbb{R}, (2.19a)
lim infx→−∞u(t,x)>0,lim infx→−∞v(t,x)>0,for allt∈ℝ.\displaystyle\liminf_{x\to-\infty}u(t,x)>0,\;\liminf_{x\to-\infty}v(t,x)>0,\ \ \text{for all}\ \ t\in\mathbb{R}. (2.19b)

The left traveling wave is defined the same way by reversing the direction of the xx-axis, namely

u(t+Lc,x)=u(t,x+L),v(t+Lc,x)=v(t,x+L),for all(t,x)∈ℝ2,u\left(t+\frac{L}{c},x\right)=u(t,x+L),\;v\left(t+\frac{L}{c},x\right)=v(t,x+L),\ \ \text{for all}\ \ (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, (2.20)

with reversed asymptotics at x=±∞x=\pm\infty.

Next we define the notion of right and left stationary wave solutions. Stationary waves, which we may also call “stationary fronts”, are the natural extension of traveling waves to the case c=0c=0.

Definition 7 (Stationary wave solutions).

Let (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(u⁡(x),v⁡(x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big)=\big(u(x),v(x)\big) be a stationary solution to (1.1), i.e. a solution that is constant in time. We say that (u⁡(x),v⁡(x))\big(u(x),v(x)\big) is a right stationary wave (or a right stationary front) if it satisfies the asymptotics (2.19) at x=±∞x=\pm\infty. A left stationary wave (or a left stationary front) is defined the same way by reversing the direction of the xx-axis, namely, it satisfies the asymptotics

limx→−∞u⁡(x)=0,limx→−∞v⁡(x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}u(x)=0,\;\lim_{x\to-\infty}v(x)=0, (2.21a)
lim infx→+∞u(x)>0,lim infx→+∞v(x)>0,for allt∈ℝ.\displaystyle\liminf_{x\to+\infty}u(x)>0,\;\liminf_{x\to+\infty}v(x)>0,\ \ \text{for all}\ \ t\in\mathbb{R}. (2.21b)

Our first main result is concerned with the existence of traveling waves. Here, the symbols cR∗c^{*}_{R} and cL∗c^{*}_{L} denote, respectively, the right and left spreading speeds defined in Definition 5.

Theorem 2.13 (Existence of traveling waves).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. Assume that cR∗>0c^{*}_{R}>0. Then there exists a right traveling wave (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) for (1.1) with speed cc if and only if c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R}. Similarly, if cL∗>0c^{*}_{L}>0, then there exists a left traveling wave (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) for (1.1) with speed cc if and only if c≥cL∗c\geq c^{*}_{L}.

Remark 2.14.

The above theorem, together with Theorem 2.7, shows that the right (resp. left) spreading speeds for solutions of (1.1) with front-like initial data coincide with the minimal speed of the right (resp. left) traveling waves provided that cR∗>0c^{*}_{R}>0 (resp. cL∗>0c^{*}_{L}>0). Note also that if cR∗>0c^{*}_{R}>0 and cL∗>0c^{*}_{L}>0, then these values coincide with the right and left spreading speeds for solutions with compactly supported initial data.

Theorem 2.15 (Existence of stationary and traveling waves).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. Assume that cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0. Then there exists a right stationary wave for (1.1). Furthermore, there exists a traveling wave (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) with speed cc if and only if c>cR∗=0c>c^{*}_{R}=0. Similarly, if cL∗=0c^{*}_{L}=0, then there exists a right stationary wave for (1.1). Furthermore, there exists a traveling wave (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) with speed cc if and only if c>cL∗=0c>c^{*}_{L}=0.

Remark 2.16.

If cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0, the propagation of any compactly supported initial data is blocked in the right direction. This is easily seen by using the exponential upper barriers (3.9) with λ=λ∗\lambda=\lambda^{*} and c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}, which do not move in space, A similar statement holds true in the left direction if cL∗=0c^{*}_{L}=0.

The proof of Theorems 2.13 and 2.15 involves a fixed-point argument at its core. More precisely, for each speed c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R}, we first restrict the system (1.1) on the moving interval −M+c​t≤x<+∞-M+ct\leq x<+\infty and prove the existence of a traveling wave for this restricted system by applying the Schauder fixed-point theorem, then we let M→∞M\to\infty to obtain a traveling wave of the original system.

In order to apply the fixed-point theorem, we construct upper and lower barriers for our system (1.1) that have the same designated decay rate as x→∞x\to\infty. This can be done despite the absence of the comparison principle for the entire system. The upper barrier is easy to construct, as it is simply a solution of the linearized system. The construction of the lower barrier is much more involved. In the supercritical case c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} it uses the difference between two exponential functions. This method is inspired by the paper of Hamel [17] for scalar equations. However, unlike the case of scalar equations, simply taking the maximum between (0,0)(0,0) and a sub-solution does not necessarily provide a lower barrier. Therefore, we need more subtle estimates in the case of systems, particularly when one of the components becomes negative while the other is still positive. In the critical case c=cR∗,cL∗c=c^{*}_{R},c^{*}_{L} our construction of the lower barrier is different from that of [17].

As mentioned earlier, our existence proof for the critical speed c=cR∗,cL∗c=c_{R}^{*},c_{L}^{*} does not depend on the limiting argument c→cR∗,cL∗c\to c_{R}^{*},c_{L}^{*}. Instead, we prove the existence for the critical case by constructing upper and lower barriers that are different from those for the super-critical case.

Figure 1 gives a typical image of traveling waves for different parameter values. In all these examples, the intrinsic growth rates satisfy ru<rvr_{u}<r_{v} so that the natural front speed of vv is faster than that of uu, while their carrying capacity (in the absence of the other species and mutation) satisfy ru/κu>rv/κvr_{u}/\kappa_{u}>r_{v}/\kappa_{v} so that uu will eventually dominate vv in the long run.

The following theorem is concerned with the decay properties of any traveling wave along the leading edge. The proof of this result is rather involved and will be given in Section 4.

Theorem 2.17 (Decay rate of traveling waves).

Let the assumptions of Theorem 2.13 hold.

  1. 1.

    Let (u,v)(u,v) be a right traveling wave solution for (1.1) with super-critical speed c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}, then there exists α>0\alpha>0 such that the following statement holds.

    limx→+∞supt∈[0,L/c]max⁡(|u⁡(t,x)​eλc​(x−c​t)−α​φλc​(x)|,|v⁡(t,x)​eλc​(x−c​t)−α​ψλc​(x)|)=0,\lim_{x\to+\infty}\sup_{t\in[0,L/c]}\max\left(\left|u(t,x)e^{\lambda_{c}(x-ct)}-\alpha\varphi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)\right|,\left|v(t,x)e^{\lambda_{c}(x-ct)}-\alpha\psi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)\right|\right)=0, (2.22)

    where λc\lambda_{c} is the smallest positive root of the equation k⁡(λ)=λ​ck(\lambda)=\lambda c and (φλc,ψλc)(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}}) denotes the principal eigenvector of (2.6) with λ=λc\lambda=\lambda_{c}.

  2. 2.

    Let (u,v)(u,v) be a right traveling wave solution for (1.1) with critical speed c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}, then there exists α>0\alpha>0 such that the following statement holds.

    limx→+∞supt∈[0,L/c]max⁡(|u⁡(t,x)​eλ∗​(x−cR∗​t)x−cR∗​t−α​φλ∗​(x)|,|v⁡(t,x)​eλ∗​(x−cR∗​t)x−cR∗​t−α​ψλ∗​(x)|)=0,\lim_{x\to+\infty}\sup_{t\in[0,L/c]}\max\left(\left|u(t,x)\frac{e^{\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}}{x-c^{*}_{R}t}-\alpha\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(x)\right|,\left|v(t,x)\frac{e^{\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}}{x-c^{*}_{R}t}-\alpha\psi^{\lambda^{*}}(x)\right|\right)=0, (2.23)

    where λ∗\lambda^{*} is the unique positive root of the equation k⁡(λ)=λ​cR∗k(\lambda)=\lambda c^{*}_{R} and (φλc,ψλc)(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}}) denotes the principal eigenvector of (2.6) with λ=λ∗\lambda=\lambda^{*}.

Similar statements hold for left traveling waves, if we replace x−c​tx-ct by x+c​tx+ct and define λc\lambda_{c} (resp. λ∗\lambda^{*}) as the largest negative solution of k⁡(λc)=−λc​ck(\lambda_{c})=-\lambda_{c}c (resp. k⁡(λ∗)=−λ∗​cL∗k(\lambda^{*})=-\lambda^{*}c^{*}_{L}).

Remark 2.18.

The assertion 1 of Theorem 2.17 remains true even if cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0, and the proof is exactly the same. The assertion 2 is also true even if cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0. More precisely, any right stationary wave satisfies (2.23) with cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0. The proof of this latter result is easier than that of Theorem 2.17 and follows from the center manifold theory for ODEs. We omit the proof here. The same is true of left traveling waves and left stationary waves if cL∗=0c^{*}_{L}=0.

The upper and lower barriers that are used in the proof of Theorem 2.13 satisfy the same decay estimates as above. In other words, in Theorem 2.13, we constructed traveling waves that satisfy these decay properties. Theorem 2.17 asserts that all the traveling waves indeed have these decay properties, therefore they are universal properties.

Next theorem is concerned with the uniqueness of traveling waves. In the case of scalar equations, the uniqueness has been proved for KPP-type equations in a much more general framework [18]. At the moment, we do not know if uniqueness generally holds in our system for each speed cc. However, under extra conditions on the coefficients, we can prove the uniqueness.

Theorem 2.19 (Uniqueness of traveling waves).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let λ1p​e​r>0\lambda_{1}^{per}>0. Assume that

κmaxκmin≤μminrmax,\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{max}}}{\kappa_{\mathrm{min}}}\leq\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{min}}}{r_{\mathrm{max}}}, (2.24)

where rmaxr_{\mathrm{max}}, κmin\kappa_{\mathrm{min}}, κmax\kappa_{\mathrm{max}}, μmin\mu_{\mathrm{min}} are as in (2.1). Then, for each c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} (resp. c>cL∗c>c^{*}_{L}), the right (resp. left) traveling wave with speed cc is unique up to a shift in time, and t↦(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))t\mapsto\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) is increasing. The same holds for c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R} (resp. c=cL∗c=c^{*}_{L}) if cR∗>0c^{*}_{R}>0 (resp. cL∗>0c^{*}_{L}>0).

We end this subsection with a result on the behavior behind the front. The profile of traveling waves of (1.1) far behind the front is not well understood except that they are bounded from above and below by positive constants. The difficulty comes from the fact that (1.1) is not entirely a cooperative system, therefore the comparison principle holds only partially. However, if the coefficients are spatially homogeneous or rapidly oscillating, we can show that the profile of any traveling wave converges to the unique positive steady state as x→−∞x\to-\infty.

We begin with the spatially homogeneous case. In this case, (1.1) is written in the form

{ut=σ​ux​x+(ru−κu​(u+v))​u+μv​v−μu​u,vt=σ​vx​x+(rv−κv​(u+v))​v+μu​u−μv​v,\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&u_{t}=\sigma u_{xx}+\big(r_{u}-\kappa_{u}(u+v)\big)u+\mu_{v}v-\mu_{u}u,\\ &v_{t}=\sigma v_{xx}+\big(r_{v}-\kappa_{v}(u+v)\big)v+\mu_{u}u-\mu_{v}v,\end{aligned}\right. (2.25)

and the linearized system (2.4) is written in the following form:

{ut−σ​ux​x=(ru−μu)​u+μv​v,vt−σ​vx​x=(rv−μv)​v+μu​u,t>0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&u_{t}-\sigma u_{xx}=(r_{u}-\mu_{u})u+\mu_{v}v,\\ &v_{t}-\sigma v_{xx}=(r_{v}-\mu_{v})v+\mu_{u}u,\end{aligned}\right.\quad t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}.

The coefficient matrix of the right-hand side of the above system is given by

A:=(ru−μuμvμurv−μv).A:=\begin{pmatrix}r_{u}-\mu_{u}&\mu_{v}\\ \mu_{u}&r_{v}-\mu_{v}\end{pmatrix}. (2.26)

Let λA\lambda_{A} denote the principal eigenvalue of AA, that is, the larger of the two eigenvalues of AA. Then it is shown in [15, (2.29)] that

k⁡(λ)=σ​λ2+λA.k(\lambda)=\sigma\lambda^{2}+\lambda_{A}.

Consequently, λA=minλ∈ℝ⁡k⁡(λ)=k⁡(0)=λ1p​e​r\lambda_{A}=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}k(\lambda)=k(0)=\lambda_{1}^{per}. In particular, if λA>0\lambda_{A}>0, then, by (2.14),

cR∗=cL∗=2​σ​λA>0.c^{*}_{R}=c^{*}_{L}=2\sqrt{\sigma\lambda_{A}}>0. (2.27)
Theorem 2.20 (Behavior behind the front: the homogeneous case).

Let the coefficients of (1.1) are all constants and let Assumption 1 hold true. Assume that λA>0\lambda_{A}>0, where λA\lambda_{A} denotes the principal eigenvalue of the matrix AA in (2.26). Then, there exists a unique positive steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}), which is spatially homogeneous. Furthermore, any right traveling wave (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big)=\big(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)\big) of (1.1) with speed c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} converges to (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) behind the front:

limξ→−∞(U⁡(ξ),V⁡(ξ))=(u∗,v∗).\lim_{\xi\to-\infty}\big(U(\xi),V(\xi)\big)=\big(u^{*},v^{*}\big). (2.28)

Similary results hold for left traveling waves.

2.3 Asymmetric propagation speed and a singular limit problem

Here we give an example for which the right and left speeds cR∗,cL∗c^{*}_{R},c^{*}_{L} are different. As we mentioned before, such a situation never occurs in scalar KPP type equations, and also not in system (1.1) if the coefficients satisfy certain symmetry conditions (Proposition 2.12).

We have shown such an example in a preprint [14], which, however, heavily relies on the fact that the diffusion coefficients of the two species are different, and cannot be adapted to the present situation. The example we present here is based on a totally different idea. We construct the example through an analysis of a certain singular limit problem.

We consider the following system which is a special case of (1.1):

{∂tu=∂x​xu+u⁡(1−κ⁡(u+v))−μ1​(x)​u+μ2​(x)​v∂tv=∂x​xv+v⁡(r−κ⁡(u+v))+μ1​(x)​u−μ2​(x)​v,\begin{cases}\ \partial_{t}u=\partial_{xx}u+u\big(1-\kappa(u+v)\big)-\mu_{1}(x)u+\mu_{2}(x)v\\[2.0pt] \ \partial_{t}v=\partial_{xx}v+v\big(r-\kappa(u+v)\big)+\mu_{1}(x)u-\mu_{2}(x)v,\end{cases} (2.35)

where κ>0,r>0\kappa>0,r>0 are positive constants, and μ1​(x),μ2​(x)\mu_{1}(x),{\mu_{2}}(x) are nonnegative LL-periodic functions that represent mutation rates and are given by:

μ1​(x)={με​δ(0≤x≤ε)0(ε<x<L),μ2​(x)={με​δ(δ−ε≤x≤δ)0(0≤x<δ−ε,δ<x<L),\mu_{1}(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mu}{\varepsilon\delta}&(0\leq x\leq\varepsilon)\\[6.0pt] 0&(\varepsilon<x<L)\end{cases},\quad\mu_{2}(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mu}{\varepsilon\delta}&(\delta-\varepsilon\leq x\leq\delta)\\[6.0pt] 0&(0\leq x<\delta-\varepsilon,\,\delta<x<L),\end{cases} (2.36)

where μ>0,δ>0\mu>0,\delta>0 and 0<ε<δ20<\varepsilon<\frac{\delta}{2} are fixed constants. Strictly speaking, this parameter choice does not satisfy assumption 1 because μu​(x)\mu_{u}(x) and μv​(x)\mu_{v}(x) take the value zero, however, we can recover assumption 1 by mollifying μu\mu_{u} and μv\mu_{v} with any positive mollifier, for instance the Gaussian kernel. We plot a schematic representation of μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} in a unit periodicity cell in Figure 2.

Our main result in this subsection is the following:

Theorem 2.22.

Assume r>1r>1 and let cR∗​(δ,ε)c^{*}_{R}(\delta,\varepsilon) and cL∗​(δ,ε)c^{*}_{L}(\delta,\varepsilon) denote the right and the left spreading speeds of (2.35)–(2.36), which are given by (2.14). Then, for all sufficiently small ε>0,δ>0\varepsilon>0,\delta>0 with ε=𝒪⁡(δ2)\varepsilon=\mathcal{O}(\delta^{2}), the following inequality holds:

cR∗​(ε,δ)<cL∗​(ε,δ).c^{*}_{R}(\varepsilon,\delta)<c^{*}_{L}(\varepsilon,\delta). (2.37)
Remark 2.23.

Note that, in the above theorem, the condition ε=O⁡(δ2)\varepsilon=O(\delta^{2}) does not mean that ε\varepsilon and δ2\delta^{2} are comparable. It simply says that ε/δ2\varepsilon/\delta^{2} remains bounded as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0. In particular, (2.37) holds if we fix a sufficiently small value of δ>0\delta>0 and let ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

To verify the claim (2.37), we have performed numerical simulations of the evolution of solution fronts of (2.35)–(2.36). As it turned out that ε\varepsilon has to be very small to see an effective difference between the two speeds in (2.37), we computed the solution of the singular limit of the system (2.35)–(2.36) as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 instead of computing the original system. The result is given in Figure 3 (upper right), which shows a noticeable difference between the right and left speeds.

Let us explain this singular limit in more detail. We fix δ>0\delta>0 in (2.36) and let ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The term −μ1​(x)​u-\mu_{1}(x)u in the first equation of (2.35) represents a big absorption of mass of the size (ε​δ)−1​μ​u(\varepsilon\delta)^{-1}\mu u over the interval [0,ε][0,\varepsilon] while the term μ2​(x)​v\mu_{2}(x)v represents a big generation of mass of the size (ε​δ)−1​μ​v(\varepsilon\delta)^{-1}\mu v over the interval [δ−ε,δ][\delta-\varepsilon,\delta]. In the second equation of (2.35), the roles of absorption and generation are reversed. As ε\varepsilon tends to 00, the effect of absorption and that of generation of mass are expressed by a flux gap of the size δ−1​μ​u\delta^{-1}\mu u or δ−1​μ​v\delta^{-1}\mu v at x=m​Lx=mL and x=m​L+δ⁡(m∈ℤ)x=mL+\delta\;(m\in{\mathbb{Z}}). Thus, at least formally, the limit problem (as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0) takes the following form:

{∂tu=∂x​xu+u⁡(1−κ⁡(u+v))x∈⋃m∈ℤ(Im∪Jm),t>0∂tv=∂x​xv+v⁡(r−κ⁡(u+v))x∈⋃m∈ℤ(Im∪Jm),t>0,\begin{cases}\ \partial_{t}u=\partial_{xx}u+u(1-\kappa(u+v))&x\in\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\left(I_{m}\cup J_{m}\right),\;t>0\\[2.0pt] \ \partial_{t}v=\partial_{xx}v+v(r-\kappa(u+v))&x\in\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\left(I_{m}\cup J_{m}\right),\;t>0,\end{cases} (2.38a)
where
Im=(m​L,m​L+δ),Jm=(m​L+δ,(m+1)​L),I_{m}=(mL,mL+\delta),\quad J_{m}=(mL+\delta,(m+1)L),
along with the following boundary conditions for all m∈ℤ,t>0m\in\mathbb{Z},\;t>0, which represent the flux gap:
{u⁡(m​L+0,t)=u⁡(m​L−0,t),ux​(m​L+0,t)=ux​(m​L−0,t)+μδ​u​(m​L,t),u⁡(m​L+δ+0,t)=u⁡(m​L+δ−0,t),ux​(m​L+δ+0,t)=ux​(m​L+δ−0,t)−μδ​v​(m​L+δ,t),\begin{cases}\ u(mL+0,t)=u(mL-0,t),\\ \ u_{x}(mL+0,t)=u_{x}(mL-0,t)+\dfrac{\mu}{\delta}\hskip 1.0ptu(mL,t),\\ \ u(mL+\delta+0,t)=u(mL+\delta-0,t),\\ \ u_{x}(mL+\delta+0,t)=u_{x}(mL+\delta-0,t)-\dfrac{\mu}{\delta}\hskip 1.0ptv(mL+\delta,t),\end{cases} (2.38b)
{v⁡(m​L+0,t)=v⁡(m​L−0,t),vx​(m​L+0,t)=vx​(m​L−0,t)−μδ​u​(m​L,t),v⁡(m​L+δ+0,t)=v⁡(m​L+δ−0,t),vx​(m​L+δ+0,t)=vx​(m​L+δ−0,t)+μδ​v​(m​L+δ,t).\begin{cases}\ v(mL+0,t)=v(mL-0,t),\\ \ v_{x}(mL+0,t)=v_{x}(mL-0,t)-\dfrac{\mu}{\delta}\hskip 1.0ptu(mL,t),\\ \ v(mL+\delta+0,t)=v(mL+\delta-0,t),\\ \ v_{x}(mL+\delta+0,t)=v_{x}(mL+\delta-0,t)+\dfrac{\mu}{\delta}\hskip 1.0ptv(mL+\delta,t).\end{cases} (2.38c)

The proof of Theorem 2.22 will be given in Section 6. In view of (2.14), it suffices to show that k⁡(λ)<k⁡(−λ)k(\lambda)<k(-\lambda) for a certain range of λ>0\lambda>0. This is a consequence of the asymmetry in the position of flux gaps. We will first establish this inequality for the limit problem as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, then show that the same inequality holds for sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0.

3 Existence and uniqueness of traveling waves

3.1 Comparison with a lower barrier

As already stated, the existence of traveling waves is proved by constructing upper and lower barriers and applying the Schauder fixed point theorem along with a limiting argument. What is most important is to find suitable lower barriers. Since our system (1.1) is not entirely cooperative, the comparison principle does not hold for the entire system. Therefore, subsolutions of (1.1) may not act as lower barriers. To overcome this difficulty, we consider an auxiliary system (3.2) below and construct lower barriers of (1.1) using this system, as we did in our previous paper [15] to study spreading properties. Note that this system has the same linearization as (1.1) along the leading edge. We introduce some key notations. Let

K:=min⁡(infx∈ℝμv​(x)κu​(x),infx∈ℝμu​(x)κv​(x)),β:=2​max⁡(supx∈ℝru​(x),supx∈ℝrv​(x))K,K:=\min\left(\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{\mu_{v}(x)}{\kappa_{u}(x)},\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{\mu_{u}(x)}{\kappa_{v}(x)}\right),\qquad\beta:={2}\,\dfrac{\max\left(\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}r_{u}(x),\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}r_{v}(x)\right)}{K}, (3.1)

and let (u~​(t,x),v~​(t,x))\big(\tilde{u}(t,x),\tilde{v}(t,x)\big) denote a solution to the auxiliary system:

{u~t=(σ⁡(x)​u~x)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u~+v~)−β​u~)​u~+μv​(x)​v~−μu​(x)​u~,t>0,x∈ℝ,v~t=(σ⁡(x)​v~x)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u~+v~)−β​v~)​v~+μu​(x)​u~−μv​(x)​v~,t>0,x∈ℝ.\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&\tilde{u}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\tilde{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(\tilde{u}+\tilde{v})-\beta\tilde{u}\big)\tilde{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\tilde{v}-\mu_{u}(x)\tilde{u},&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &\tilde{v}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\tilde{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(\tilde{u}+\tilde{v})-\beta\tilde{v}\big)\tilde{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\tilde{u}-\mu_{v}(x)\tilde{v},&t>0,x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{aligned}\right. (3.2)
Lemma 3.1 (Comparison with a lower barrier).

Let Assumption 1 hold true. Let u~0​(x)\tilde{u}_{0}(x) and v~0​(x)\tilde{v}_{0}(x) be continuous functions such that

0≤u~0​(x)≤min⁡(u0​(x),12​K)and​ 0≤v~0​(x)≤min⁡(v0​(x),12​K),0\leq\tilde{u}_{0}(x)\leq\min\big(u_{0}(x),\frac{1}{2}K\big)\ \ \text{and}\ \ 0\leq\tilde{v}_{0}(x)\leq\min\big(v_{0}(x),\frac{1}{2}K\big), (3.3)

and let (u~​(t,x),v~​(t,x))\big(\tilde{u}(t,x),\tilde{v}(t,x)\big) be the solution of (3.2) starting from u~​(0,x)=u~0​(x)\tilde{u}(0,x)=\tilde{u}_{0}(x) and v~​(0,x)=v~0​(x)\tilde{v}(0,x)=\tilde{v}_{0}(x). Then for all t>0t>0 and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} we have

u~​(t,x)≤u⁡(t,x)andv~​(t,x)≤v⁡(t,x).\tilde{u}(t,x)\leq u(t,x)\ \ \text{and}\ \ \tilde{v}(t,x)\leq v(t,x). (3.4)
Proof.

We refer to our previous paper [15, Lemma 9]. ∎

3.2 Proof of existence

The goal of this section is to prove Theorems 2.13 and 2.15 on the existence of traveling waves and stationary waves. We consider only the right traveling waves and stationary waves, as the left ones can be treated precisely the same way. We seek traveling waves that have a precise decay rate when x→+∞x\to+\infty, that is anticipated by the linear analysis near the leading edge. Later, in Theorem 2.17, we will see that these decay properties are universal for all traveling waves. As we mentioned earlier, the existence will be proved by a fixed-point argument. More precisely, for each speed c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R}, we first restrict the system (1.1) on the moving interval −M+c​t≤x<+∞-M+ct\leq x<+\infty and prove the existence of a traveling wave for this restricted system by applying the Schauder fixed-point theorem, then we let M→∞M\to\infty to obtain a traveling wave of the original system.

In order to apply the fixed-point theorem, we need to construct upper and lower barriers. The upper barrier is easy to construct, as it is simply a solution of the linearized system. On the other hand, the construction of the lower barrier is much more involved. Our construction of lower barriers for c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} is partly adapted from [17] on scalar equations, but the lower barrier for c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R} is different from [17] and is new, even for scalar KPP equations.

As a matter of fact, it is possible to prove the existence of traveling waves for the critical case c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R} by a limiting argument, namely by taking the limit as c→cR∗c\to c^{*}_{R} of the traveling waves of speed c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}. Such an approach is more common in the study of scalar equations, but it does not give detailed information about the spatial decay rate of the critical traveling wave as x→+∞x\to+\infty. Our approach, on the other hand, gives an optimal decay rate directly for the case c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}.

Now, for each fixed M≥0M\geq 0 and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, let us consider the following system, which is obtained by restricting the system (1.1) on the interval −M+c​t≤x<+∞-M+ct\leq x<+\infty:

{ut=(σ⁡(x)​ux)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u+v))​u+μv​(x)​v−μu​(x)​u,t>0,x>−M+ct,vt=(σ⁡(x)​vx)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u+v))​v+μu​(x)​u−μv​(x)​v,t>0,x>−M+ct,ux​(t,−M+c​t)=vx​(t,−M+c​t)=0(t>0).\left\{\begin{aligned} {}&u_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)u_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(u+v)\big)u+\mu_{v}(x)v-\mu_{u}(x)u,&t>0,\,x>-M+ct,\\ &v_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)v_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(u+v)\big)v+\mu_{u}(x)u-\mu_{v}(x)v,&t>0,\,x>-M+ct,\\ &u_{x}(t,-M+ct)=v_{x}(t,-M+ct)=0\quad\ (t>0).\end{aligned}\right. (3.5)

The global existence and the uniqueness of solutions of system (3.5) for nonnegative bounded continuous initial data (u0​(x),v0​(x))\big(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)\big) is classical. We next consider the following auxiliary system which is obtained by restricting (3.2) on the interval −M+c​t≤x<+∞-M+ct\leq x<+\infty:

{u~t=(σ⁡(x)​u~x)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u~+v~)−β​u~)​u~+μv​(x)​v~−μu​(x)​u~,v~t=(σ⁡(x)​v~x)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u~+v~)−β​v~)​v~+μu​(x)​u~−μv​(x)​v~,u~x​(t,−M+c​t)=v~x​(t,−M+c​t)=0(t>0).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\tilde{u}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\tilde{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(\tilde{u}+\tilde{v})-\beta\tilde{u}\big)\tilde{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\tilde{v}-\mu_{u}(x)\tilde{u},\\ &\tilde{v}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\tilde{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(\tilde{u}+\tilde{v})-\beta\tilde{v}\big)\tilde{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\tilde{u}-\mu_{v}(x)\tilde{v},\\ &\tilde{u}_{x}(t,-M+ct)=\tilde{v}_{x}(t,-M+ct)=0\quad(t>0).\end{aligned}\right. (3.6)

Then equivalents of Proposition 2.2 and Lemma 3.1 hold for this system, with virtually the same proof except for a minor modification at the boundary x=−M+c​tx=-M+ct. We state below an equivalent of Lemma 3.1 without proof.

Lemma 3.2 (Comparison with a lower barrier).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let M≥0M\geq 0 and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} be given, and let K¯\overline{K} be as in (2.1). Let (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) be a solution of (3.5) whose initial data (u0​(x),v0​(x))\big(u_{0}(x),v_{0}(x)\big) is bounded, nonnegative and continuous, and let u~0​(x)\tilde{u}_{0}(x) and v~0​(x)\tilde{v}_{0}(x) be continuous functions such that

0≤u~0​(x):=min⁡(u0​(x),12​K)​ and ​0≤v~0​(x)≤min⁡(v0​(x),12​K).0\leq\tilde{u}_{0}(x):=\min\big(u_{0}(x),\frac{1}{2}K\big)\text{ and }0\leq\tilde{v}_{0}(x)\leq\min\big(v_{0}(x),\frac{1}{2}K\big). (3.7)

Then the solution (u~​(t,x),v~​(t,x))\big(\tilde{u}(t,x),\tilde{v}(t,x)\big) of (3.6) with initial data (u~0​(x),v~0​(x))\big(\tilde{u}_{0}(x),\tilde{v}_{0}(x)\big) satisfies

u~​(t,x)≤u⁡(t,x)andv~​(t,x)≤v⁡(t,x)for allt>0,x≥−M+c​t.\tilde{u}(t,x)\leq u(t,x)\ \ \text{and}\ \ \tilde{v}(t,x)\leq v(t,x)\ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ t>0,\ x\geq-M+ct. (3.8)

The following Proposition gives an upper barrier for the supercritical case.

Proposition 3.3 (Upper barrier).

Let Assumption 1 hold true, K¯\overline{K} be as in (2.1) and M≥0M\geq 0 be given. Let λ>0\lambda>0 and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} be such that c≥k⁡(λ)λc\geq\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}. Define

u¯​(t,x):=e−λ⁡(x−c​t)​φλ​(x)v¯​(t,x):=e−λ⁡(x−c​t)​ψλ​(x),\overline{u}(t,x):=e^{-\lambda(x-ct)}{\varphi}^{\lambda}(x)\quad\overline{v}(t,x):=e^{-\lambda(x-ct)}{\psi}^{\lambda}(x), (3.9)

where (φλ,ψλ)(\varphi^{\lambda},\psi^{\lambda}) is the λ\lambda-periodic principal eigenvector of (2.6) that satisfies ‖(φλ,ψλ)‖L∞=1\|({\varphi}^{\lambda},\psi^{\lambda})\|_{L^{\infty}}=1.

If MM is sufficiently large, then for any solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) of (3.5) satisfying u​(0,x)≤u¯​(0,x)u(0,x)\leq\overline{u}(0,x), v​(0,x)≤v¯​(0,x)v(0,x)\leq\overline{v}(0,x), u⁡(0,x)+v⁡(0,x)≤K¯u(0,x)+v(0,x)\leq\overline{K}, it holds that

u(t,x)≤u¯(t,x),v(t,x)≤v¯(t,x),u(t,x)+v(t,x)≤K¯for allt≥0,x≥−M+ct.u(t,x)\leq\overline{u}(t,x),\ \ v(t,x)\leq\overline{v}(t,x),\ \ u(t,x)+v(t,x)\leq\overline{K}\ \ \hbox{for all}\ \ t\geq 0,\ x\geq-M+ct.
Proof.

The fact that u⁡(t,x)+v⁡(t,x)≤K¯u(t,x)+v(t,x)\leq\overline{K} is a consequence of (an equivalent of) Proposition 2.2, so we prove the former two inequalities. Direct computation show that

u¯t=(σ⁡(x)​u¯x)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x)+λ​c−k⁡(λ))​u¯+μv​(x)​v¯,\displaystyle\overline{u}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\overline{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)+\lambda c-k(\lambda)\big)\overline{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\overline{v}, (3.10)
v¯t=(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x)+λ​c−k⁡(λ))​v¯+μu​(x)​u¯.\displaystyle\overline{v}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\overline{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)+\lambda c-k(\lambda)\big)\overline{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\overline{u}.

Therefore (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}) is a solution of the linear cooperative system (3.10). Since c≥k⁡(λ)λc\geq\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}, we have

ut\displaystyle{u}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​ux)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x)−κu​(x)​(u+v))​u+μv​(x)​v\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(u+v)\big){u}+\mu_{v}(x){v}
≤(σ⁡(x)​ux)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x)+λ​c−k⁡(λ))​u+μv​(x)​v,\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x){u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)+\lambda c-k(\lambda)\big){u}+\mu_{v}(x){v},
vt\displaystyle{v}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​vx)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u+v))​v+μu​(x)​u\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(u+v)\big){v}+\mu_{u}(x){u}
≤(σ⁡(x)​vx)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x)+λ​c−k⁡(λ))​v+μu​(x)​u.\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x){v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)+\lambda c-k(\lambda)\big){v}+\mu_{u}(x){u}.

Hence (u,v)(u,v) is a subsolution to the system (3.10). Moreover, for MM sufficiently large, we have

u¯​(t,−M+c​t)=eλ​M​φλ​(−M+c​t)≥K¯≥u⁡(t,−M+c​t)\overline{u}(t,-M+ct)=e^{\lambda M}\varphi^{\lambda}(-M+ct)\geq\overline{K}\geq u(t,-M+ct)

and similarly v¯​(t,−M+c​t)≥v⁡(t,−M+c​t).\overline{v}(t,-M+ct)\geq v(t,-M+ct). Thus by the comparison principle for cooperative parabolic systems, the following inequalities hold, which prove the lemma:

u(t,x)≤u¯(t,x),v(t,x)≤v¯(t,x)for allt≥0,x≥−M+ct.∎u(t,x)\leq\overline{u}(t,x),\ \ v(t,x)\leq\overline{v}(t,x)\quad\text{for all}\ \ t\geq 0,\ x\geq-M+ct.\qed

Before we construct a lower barrier, we prepare the following Lemma.

Lemma 3.4 (A differential inequality for c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} be given. Let λ>0\lambda>0 be the smallest positive solution of k⁡(λ)λ=c{\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}=c}. Define

u¯​(t,x):=e−λ⁡(x−c​t)​φλ​(x)−ω​e−ν⁡(x−c​t)​φν​(x),v¯​(t,x):=e−λ⁡(x−c​t)​ψλ​(x)−ω​e−ν⁡(x−c​t)​ψν​(x),\underline{u}(t,x):=e^{-\lambda(x-ct)}\varphi^{\lambda}(x)-\omega e^{-\nu(x-ct)}\varphi^{\nu}(x),\ \ \underline{v}(t,x):=e^{-\lambda(x-ct)}\psi^{\lambda}(x)-\omega e^{-\nu(x-ct)}\psi^{\nu}(x), (3.11)

where the constant ν>0\nu>0 satisfies k⁡(ν)−ν​c<0{k(\nu)-\nu c<0} and λ<ν<2​λ\lambda<\nu<2\lambda. Then there exists ω∗>0\omega^{*}>0 such that, for all ω≥ω∗\omega\geq\omega^{*}, we have

u¯t\displaystyle\underline{u}_{t} ≤(σ⁡(x)​u¯x)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u¯+v¯)−β​u¯)​u¯+μv​(x)​v¯−μu​(x)​u¯,\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})-\beta\underline{u}\big)\underline{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}-\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}, (3.12a)
v¯t\displaystyle\underline{v}_{t} ≤(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u¯+v¯)−β​v¯)​v¯+μu​(x)​u¯−μv​(x)​v¯,\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})-\beta\underline{v}\big)\underline{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}-\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}, (3.12b)

whenever

x−c​t>ξω:=1ν−λ​(ln⁡(ω)+ln⁡[infy∈ℝ​min⁡(φν​(y)φλ​(y),ψν​(y)ψλ​(y))]),x-ct>\xi_{\omega}:=\frac{1}{\nu-\lambda}\left(\ln(\omega)+\ln\left[\underset{{y\in\mathbb{R}}}{\inf}\min\left(\frac{\varphi^{\nu}(y)}{\varphi^{\lambda}(y)},\frac{\psi^{\nu}(y)}{\psi^{\lambda}(y)}\right)\right]\right), (3.13)

and u¯​(t,x)<0\underline{u}(t,x)<0 and v¯​(t,x)<0\underline{v}(t,x)<0 whenever x−c​t≤ξωx-ct\leq\xi_{\omega}.

Proof.

That u¯​(t,x)<0\underline{u}(t,x)<0 and v¯​(t,x)<0\underline{v}(t,x)<0 when x−c​t≤ξωx-ct\leq\xi_{\omega} follows from direct computations with the explicit formula (3.11). Let us prove the differential inequality. We have:

u¯t=(σ⁡(x)​u¯x)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x))​u¯+μv​(x)​v¯−(−k⁡(ν)+ν​c)​ω​e−ν⁡(x−c​t)​φν​(x),\displaystyle\underline{u}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\underline{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)\big)\underline{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}-(-k(\nu)+\nu c)\omega e^{-\nu(x-ct)}\varphi^{\nu}(x),
v¯t=(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x))​v¯+μu​(x)​u¯−(−k⁡(ν)+ν​c)​ω​e−ν⁡(x−c​t)​ψν​(x),\displaystyle\underline{v}_{t}=\big(\sigma(x)\underline{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)\big)\underline{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}-(-k(\nu)+\nu c)\omega e^{-\nu(x-ct)}\psi^{\nu}(x),

where we recall that −k⁡(ν)+ν​c>0-k(\nu)+\nu c>0. Observe that

κu​(x)​(u¯+v¯)​u¯+β​u¯2\displaystyle\kappa_{u}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})\underline{u}+\beta\underline{u}^{2} ≤(supκu+β)​u¯2+κu​(x)2​(u¯2+v¯2)≤(32​supκu+β)​u¯2+12​supκu​v¯2\displaystyle\leq\big(\sup\kappa_{u}+\beta\big)\underline{u}^{2}+\frac{\kappa_{u}(x)}{2}\big(\underline{u}^{2}+\underline{v}^{2}\big)\leq\left(\frac{3}{2}\sup\kappa_{u}+\beta\right)\underline{u}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sup\kappa_{u}\underline{v}^{2}
≤(2​supκu+β)​max⁡(supφλ,supψλ)2​e−2​λ​(x−c​t)\displaystyle\leq\big(2\sup\kappa_{u}+\beta\big)\max\big(\sup\varphi^{\lambda},\sup\psi^{\lambda}\big)^{2}e^{-2\lambda(x-ct)}

≤C1ω2​λ−νν−λ​φν​(x)​e−ν⁡(x−c​t),\displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{1}}{\omega^{\frac{2\lambda-\nu}{\nu-\lambda}}}\varphi^{\nu}(x)e^{-\nu(x-ct)},

since x−c​t≥ξωx-ct\geq\xi_{\omega}, where the constant C1>0C_{1}>0 depends on supκu,β,λ,ν,φλ\sup\kappa_{u},\beta,\lambda,\nu,\varphi^{\lambda} and φν\varphi^{\nu}. and therefore

κu​(x)​(u¯+v¯)​u¯+β​u¯2≤ω⁡(−k⁡(ν)+ν​c)​φν​(x)​e−ν⁡(x−c​t).\kappa_{u}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})\underline{u}+\beta\underline{u}^{2}\leq\omega(-k(\nu)+\nu c)\varphi^{\nu}(x)e^{-\nu(x-ct)}.

u¯t≤(σ⁡(x)​u¯x)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x)−κu​(x)​(u¯+v¯)−β​u¯)​u¯+μv​(x)​v¯.\underline{u}_{t}\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{u}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})-\beta\underline{u}\big)\underline{u}+\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}.

κv​(x)​(u¯+v¯)​v¯+β​v¯2≤ω⁡(−k⁡(ν)+ν​c)​ψν​(x)​e−ν⁡(x−c​t),\kappa_{v}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})\underline{v}+\beta\underline{v}^{2}\leq\omega(-k(\nu)+\nu c)\psi^{\nu}(x)e^{-\nu(x-ct)},

hence

v¯t≤(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u¯+v¯)−β​v¯)​v¯+μu​(x)​u¯.\underline{v}_{t}\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{v}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(\underline{u}+\underline{v})-\beta\underline{v}\big)\underline{v}+\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}.

Therefore, (3.12) holds true for x−c​t≥ξωx-ct\geq\xi_{\omega}, which finishes the proof of Lemma 3.4. ∎

Proposition 3.5 (Lower barrier for c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let M≥0M\geq 0, c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} be given. Let λ>0\lambda>0 be the smallest positive solution of k⁡(λ)λ=c{\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}=c} and let (u¯​(t,x),v¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{u}(t,x),\underline{v}(t,x)\big) be the defined by (3.11), where the constant ν>0\nu>0 satisfies k⁡(ν)−ν​c<0{k(\nu)-\nu c<0} and λ<ν<2​λ\lambda<\nu<2\lambda. There exists ω∗>0\omega^{*}>0 such that, for all ω≥ω∗\omega\geq\omega^{*}, we have u¯​(t,−M+c​t)<0\underline{u}(t,-M+ct)<0 and v¯​(t,−M+c​t)<0\underline{v}(t,-M+ct)<0 for all t≥0t\geq 0, and that, for any n∈{0,…,⌊ML⌋}n\in\big\{0,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac{M}{L}\right\rfloor\big\} and any nonnegative solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) of (3.5) satisfying

u0(x)≥u¯(0,x+nL),v0(x)≥v¯(0,x+nL)for allx≥−M,u_{0}(x)\geq\underline{u}(0,x+nL),\ \ v_{0}(x)\geq\underline{v}(0,x+nL)\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ x\geq-M,

we have

u(t,x)≥u¯(t,x+nL),v(t,x)≥v¯(t,x+nL)for allt≥0,x≥−M+ct.u(t,x)\geq\underline{u}(t,x+nL),\ \ v(t,x)\geq\underline{v}(t,x+nL)\quad\text{for all}\ \ t\geq 0,\ x\geq-M+ct. (3.14)

The following proof is adapted from [17] on scalar KPP type equations.

Proof.

We first prove the lemma for the special case n=0n=0, then discuss the general case later.

Let us first remark that u¯​(t+Lc,x)=u¯​(t,x−L)\underline{u}(t+\frac{L}{c},x)=\underline{u}(t,x-L) and v¯​(t+Lc,x)=v¯​(t,x−L)\underline{v}(t+\frac{L}{c},x)=\underline{v}(t,x-L). It follows from direct computations that supt,xu¯\sup_{t,x}\underline{u} and supt,xv¯\sup_{t,x}\underline{v} are both finite and become arbitrarily small when ω→+∞\omega\to+\infty. By Lemma 3.2, it suffices to check that the vector function (u¯,v¯)(\underline{u},\underline{v}) is a lower barrier to the system (3.6) if ω>0\omega>0 is sufficiently large. We assume that

ω>exp⁡(−ln⁡[infy∈ℝ​min⁡(φν​(y)φλ​(y),ψν​(y)ψλ​(y))])=(infy∈ℝ​min⁡(φν​(y)φλ​(y),ψν​(y)ψλ​(y)))−1\omega>\exp\left(-\ln\left[\underset{{y\in\mathbb{R}}}{\inf}\min\left(\frac{\varphi^{\nu}(y)}{\varphi^{\lambda}(y)},\frac{\psi^{\nu}(y)}{\psi^{\lambda}(y)}\right)\right]\right)=\left(\underset{{y\in\mathbb{R}}}{\inf}\min\left(\frac{\varphi^{\nu}(y)}{\varphi^{\lambda}(y)},\frac{\psi^{\nu}(y)}{\psi^{\lambda}(y)}\right)\right)^{-1}

so that ξω≥0\xi_{\omega}\geq 0 and in particular u¯​(t,x)<0\underline{u}(t,x)<0 and v¯​(t,x)<0\underline{v}(t,x)<0 at the boundary x=c​t−Mx=ct-M. The differential inequality for x−c​t>ξωx-ct>\xi_{\omega} follows from Lemma 3.4 and the lemma is proved for n=0n=0.

Precisely the same argument holds for (u¯​(t,x+n​L),v¯​(t,x+n​L))(\underline{u}(t,x+nL),\underline{v}(t,x+nL)\big) since these functions satisfy the same differential inequalities as the case n=0n=0 and since u¯​(t,x+n​L)<0\underline{u}(t,x+nL)<0 and v¯​(t,x+n​L)<0\underline{v}(t,x+nL)<0 at the boundary x=−M+c​tx=-M+ct for all n=1,…,⌊ML⌋n=1,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac{M}{L}\right\rfloor. This latter claim holds because u¯​(t,x)<0\underline{u}(t,x)<0 and v¯​(t,x)<0\underline{v}(t,x)<0 whenever x−c​t<0x-ct<0 by our choice of ω\omega. This completes the proof of Lemma 3.5. ∎

To construct upper and lower barriers for the critical speed c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}, we need a different approach, since the decay rate of the traveling wave as x→+∞x\to+\infty is not purely exponential. Let λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 be the unique positive solution of k⁡(λ)λ=cR∗{\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}=c^{*}_{R}}, and define

U⁡(t,x):=−∂∂λ​(e−λ⁡(x−cR∗​t)​φλ​(x))|λ=λ∗,V⁡(t,x):=−∂∂λ​(e−λ⁡(x−cR∗​t)​φλ​(x))|λ=λ∗,U(t,x):=-\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\big(e^{-\lambda(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\varphi^{\lambda}(x)\big)\big|_{\lambda=\lambda^{*}},\quad V(t,x):=-\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\big(e^{-\lambda(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\varphi^{\lambda}(x)\big)\big|_{\lambda=\lambda^{*}}, (3.15)

and, for positive constants α>0\alpha>0, ω>0\omega>0 and λ∗<ν<2​λ∗\lambda^{*}<\nu<2\lambda^{*},

u¯∗​(t,x):=U⁡(t,x)+α​e−λ∗​(x−cR∗​t)​φλ∗​(x),v¯∗​(t,x):=V⁡(t,x)+α​e−λ∗​(x−cR∗​t)​ψλ∗​(x),\begin{split}&\overline{u}^{*}(t,x):=U(t,x)+\alpha e^{-\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(x),\\ &\overline{v}^{*}(t,x):=V(t,x)+\alpha e^{-\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\psi^{\lambda^{*}}(x),\end{split} (3.16)
u¯∗​(t,x):=U⁡(t,x)+e−ν⁡(x−cR∗​t)​φν​(x)−ω​e−λ∗​(x−cR∗​t)​φλ∗​(x),v¯∗​(t,x):=V⁡(t,x)+e−ν⁡(x−cR∗​t)​ψν​(x)−ω​e−λ∗​(x−cR∗​t)​ψλ∗​(x).\begin{split}&\underline{u}^{*}(t,x):=U(t,x)+e^{-\nu(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\varphi^{\nu}(x)-\omega e^{-\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(x),\\ &\underline{v}^{*}(t,x):=V(t,x)+e^{-\nu(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\psi^{\nu}(x)-\omega e^{-\lambda^{*}(x-c^{*}_{R}t)}\psi^{\lambda^{*}}(x).\end{split} (3.17)

We will show that these functions play the role of an upper and a lower barrier for the critical case.

Lemma 3.6 (A differential inequality for c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 be the unique positive solution of k⁡(λ)λ=cR∗{\frac{k(\lambda)}{\lambda}=c^{*}_{R}}. Let ν∈(λ∗,2​λ∗)\nu\in(\lambda^{*},2\lambda^{*}) be given and α>0\alpha>0 be fixed.

  1. 1.

    The vector function (u¯∗,v¯∗)\big(\overline{u}^{*},\overline{v}^{*}\big) defined by (3.16) satisfies

    u¯t∗\displaystyle\overline{u}^{*}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​u¯x∗)x+ru​(x)​u¯∗+μv​(x)​v¯∗−μu​(x)​u¯∗,\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x)\overline{u}^{*}_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{u}(x)\overline{u}^{*}+\mu_{v}(x)\overline{v}^{*}-\mu_{u}(x)\overline{u}^{*}, (3.18a)
    v¯t∗\displaystyle\overline{v}^{*}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​v¯x∗)x+rv​(x)​v¯∗+μu​(x)​u¯∗−μv​(x)​v¯∗.\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x)\overline{v}^{*}_{x}\big)_{x}+r_{v}(x)\overline{v}^{*}+\mu_{u}(x)\overline{u}^{*}-\mu_{v}(x)\overline{v}^{*}. (3.18b)
  2. 2.

    Then there exists ω∗>0\omega^{*}>0 such that, for all ω≥ω∗\omega\geq\omega^{*}, the vector function (u¯∗,v¯∗)\big(\underline{u}^{*},\underline{v}^{*}\big) defined by (3.17) satisfies the differential inequality

    u¯t∗\displaystyle\underline{u}^{*}_{t} ≤(σ⁡(x)​u¯x∗)x+(ru​(x)−κu​(x)​(u¯∗+v¯∗)−β​u¯∗)​u¯∗+μv​(x)​v¯∗−μu​(x)​u¯∗,\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{u}^{*}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)(\underline{u}^{*}+\underline{v}^{*})-\beta\underline{u}^{*}\big)\underline{u}^{*}+\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}^{*}-\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}^{*}, (3.19a)
    v¯t∗\displaystyle\underline{v}^{*}_{t} ≤(σ⁡(x)​v¯x∗)x+(rv​(x)−κv​(x)​(u¯∗+v¯∗)−β​v¯∗)​v¯∗+μu​(x)​u¯∗−μv​(x)​v¯∗,\displaystyle\leq\big(\sigma(x)\underline{v}^{*}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)(\underline{u}^{*}+\underline{v}^{*})-\beta\underline{v}^{*}\big)\underline{v}^{*}+\mu_{u}(x)\underline{u}^{*}-\mu_{v}(x)\underline{v}^{*}, (3.19b)

    whenever

    x−cR∗​t>ξω∗:=ω+infy∈ℝ[∂φλ|λ∗​(y)φλ∗​(y)−φν​(y)φλ∗​(y)]x-c^{*}_{R}t>\xi_{\omega}^{*}:=\omega+\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\left[\frac{\partial\varphi^{\lambda}|_{\lambda^{*}}(y)}{\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(y)}-\frac{\varphi^{\nu}(y)}{\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(y)}\right] (3.20)

    and u¯∗​(t,x)<0\underline{u}^{*}(t,x)<0 and v¯∗​(t,x)<0\underline{v}^{*}(t,x)<0 whenever 0≤x−cR∗​t≤ξω∗0\leq x-c^{*}_{R}t\leq\xi_{\omega}^{*}.

Proof.

To obtain equality (3.18), we first differentiate (3.10) with respect to λ\lambda and evaluate at λ=λ∗\lambda=\lambda^{*}, which yields

Ut\displaystyle{U}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​Ux)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x)+cR∗−k′​(λ∗))​U+μv​(x)​V\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){U}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)+c^{*}_{R}-k^{\prime}(\lambda^{*})\big){U}+\mu_{v}(x){V} (3.21)
=(σ⁡(x)​Ux)x+(ru​(x)−μu​(x))​U+μv​(x)​V,\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){U}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)\big){U}+\mu_{v}(x){V},
Vt\displaystyle{V}_{t} =(σ⁡(x)​Vx)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x)+cR∗−k′​(λ∗))​V+μu​(x)​U\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){V}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)+c^{*}_{R}-k^{\prime}(\lambda^{*})\big){V}+\mu_{u}(x){U}
=(σ⁡(x)​Vx)x+(rv​(x)−μv​(x))​V+μu​(x)​U.\displaystyle=\big(\sigma(x){V}_{x}\big)_{x}+\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)\big){V}+\mu_{u}(x){U}.
