Proof of Theorem 2.13.

Let cR∗>0c^{*}_{R}>0 be the right spreading speed defined in (2.14). The fact that there exists no traveling wave for c<cR∗c<c^{*}_{R} is a direct consequence of the spreading property (Theorem 2.7). The existence of a traveling wave for c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} will be shown by using the Schauder fixed-point Theorem and a limiting argument.

We begin with the case c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}. Fix c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}, and let λ\lambda be the smallest positive solution to λ​c=k⁡(λ){\lambda c=k(\lambda)}. We let u¯​(t,x)\overline{u}(t,x) and v¯​(t,x)\overline{v}(t,x) be the functions defined in Lemma 3.3 by (3.9) and u¯​(t,x)\underline{u}(t,x) and v¯​(t,x)\underline{v}(t,x) be the function defined in Lemma 3.5 by (3.11).

For M>0M>0, let NM:=⌊ML⌋N_{M}:=\lfloor\frac{M}{L}\rfloor, i.e., the largest integer not exceeding ML\frac{M}{L}, and let EME_{M} be the (convex) set of all vector functions (u0,v0)∈BUC([−M,+∞))2(u_{0},v_{0})\in BUC\big([-M,+\infty)\big)^{2} satisfying the following constraints:

u0​(x)≥0,maxn∈{0,1,…,NM}⁡u¯​(0,x+n​L)≤u0​(x)≤u¯​(0,x),v0​(x)≥0,maxn∈{0,1,…,NM}⁡v¯​(0,x+n​L)≤v0​(x)≤v¯​(0,x),u0​(x)+v0​(x)≤K¯,}x∀≥−M,\left.\begin{aligned} u_{0}(x)&\geq 0,&\max_{n\in\{0,1,\ldots,N_{M}\}}\underline{u}(0,x+nL)\leq u_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{u}(0,x),\\ v_{0}(x)&\geq 0,&\max_{n\in\{0,1,\ldots,N_{M}\}}\underline{v}(0,x+nL)\leq v_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{v}(0,x),\\ &&u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{K},\end{aligned}\ \ \ \right\}\ \ \ {}^{\forall}x\geq-M,

where K¯\overline{K} is as in (2.1). Note that EME_{M} is not empty. Indeed, since u¯​(0,x)>u¯​(0,x)\overline{u}(0,x)>\underline{u}(0,x) and since u¯​(0,x+n​L)\overline{u}(0,x+nL) is monotone decreasing with respect to n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we clearly have u¯​(x,0)>u¯​(x+n​L)\overline{u}(x,0)>\underline{u}(x+nL) for all n≥0n\geq 0, and the same holds between v¯\overline{v} and v¯\underline{v}. Next we define an operator QM:EM→BUC([−M,+∞))2Q^{M}:E_{M}\to BUC\big([-M,+\infty)\big)^{2} by

QM​(u0,v0)​(x)=(u⁡(Lc,x+L),v⁡(Lc,x+L)),Q^{M}(u_{0},v_{0})(x)=\left(u\left(\frac{L}{c},x+L\right),v\left(\frac{L}{c},x+L\right)\right), (3.31)

where (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) is the solution of the system (3.5) starting from the initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}).

Then, it follows from Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 that QM​(EM)⊂EMQ^{M}(E_{M})\subset E_{M}. Moreover the operator QMQ^{M} is compact. Thus, the Schauder fixed-point Theorem implies the existence of a fixed-point (uM,vM)∈EM\big(u^{M},v^{M}\big)\in E_{M} such that QM​(uM,vM)=(uM,vM)Q^{M}(u^{M},v^{M})=(u^{M},v^{M}). Again by the parabolic regularity, there exists a sequence Mn→+∞M_{n}\to+\infty such that uMnu^{M_{n}} converges locally uniformly to a solution u∞{u}^{\infty} to Q∞​(u∞,v∞)=(u∞,v∞)Q^{\infty}(u^{\infty},v^{\infty})=(u^{\infty},v^{\infty}), which belongs to the set E∞⊂B​U​C​(ℝ)2E_{\infty}\subset BUC(\mathbb{R})^{2} defined by the constraints

u0​(x)≥0,supn∈ℕu¯​(0,x+n​L)≤u0​(x)≤u¯​(0,x),v0​(x)≥0,supn∈ℕv¯​(0,x+n​L)≤v0​(x)≤v¯​(0,x),u0​(x)+v0​(x)≤K¯,}x∀∈ℝ.\left.\begin{aligned} u_{0}(x)&\geq 0,&\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{u}(0,x+nL)\leq u_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{u}(0,x),\\ v_{0}(x)&\geq 0,&\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{v}(0,x+nL)\leq v_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{v}(0,x),\\ &&u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x)&\leq\overline{K},\end{aligned}\ \ \ \right\}\ \ \ {}^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}.

Note first that the equality Q∞​(u∞,v∞)=(u∞,v∞)Q^{\infty}(u^{\infty},v^{\infty})=(u^{\infty},v^{\infty}) is equivalent to (2.18). Next, since u¯​(t,x)→0\overline{u}(t,x)\to 0 and v¯​(t,x)→0\overline{v}(t,x)\to 0 as x→+∞x\to+\infty, we have u∞​(t,x)→0u^{\infty}(t,x)\to 0, v∞​(t,x)→0v^{\infty}(t,x)\to 0 as x→+∞x\to+\infty, which proves (2.19a). The condition (2.19b) is satisfied since supn∈ℕu¯​(t,x+n​L)\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{u}(t,x+nL) and supn∈ℕv¯​(t,x+n​L)\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{v}(t,x+nL) are uniformly bounded below by positive constants as x→−∞x\to-\infty. Thus (u∞,v∞)(u^{\infty},v^{\infty}) is the expected traveling wave.

Next we consider the case c=cR∗>0c=c^{*}_{R}>0. In this case, we can basically repeat the same procedure, replacing EME_{M} by the set EM∗⊂BUC([−M,+∞))2E_{M}^{*}\subset BUC\big([-M,+\infty)\big)^{2} defined by the constraints

u0(x)≥0,v0(x)≥0,u0(x)+v0(x)≤K¯,∀x≥−M;u0(x)≤u¯∗(0,x),v0(x)≤u¯∗(0,x),∀x≥ξ0;u¯∗M(x)≤u0(x),v¯∗M(x)≤v0(x),∀x≥ξ0−NML,\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ v_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x)\leq\overline{K},&{}^{\forall}x\geq-M;\\[6.0pt] u_{0}(x)\leq\overline{u}^{*}(0,x),\quad\ v_{0}(x)\leq\overline{u}^{*}(0,x),&{}^{\forall}x\geq\xi_{0};\\[6.0pt] \underline{u}^{*}_{M}(x)\leq u_{0}(x),\quad\ \ \underline{v}^{*}_{M}(x)\leq v_{0}(x),&{}^{\forall}x\geq\xi_{0}-N_{M}L,\end{array}

where

u¯M∗​(x):=maxn∈{0,1,…,NM}⁡u¯∗​(0,x+n​L),v¯M∗​(x):=maxn∈{0,1,…,NM}⁡v¯∗​(0,x+n​L).\underline{u}^{*}_{M}(x):=\max\limits_{n\in\{0,1,\ldots,N_{M}\}}\underline{u}^{*}(0,x+nL),\quad\underline{v}^{*}_{M}(x):=\max\limits_{n\in\{0,1,\ldots,N_{M}\}}\underline{v}^{*}(0,x+nL).

Note that EM∗≠∅E^{*}_{M}\neq\varnothing since u¯∗​(0,x)>u¯∗​(0,x)\overline{u}^{*}(0,x)>\underline{u}^{*}(0,x) and u¯∗​(0,x+n​L)\overline{u}^{*}(0,x+nL) is monotone decreasing with respect to n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The operator QM:EM∗→EM∗Q^{M}:E_{M}^{*}\to E_{M}^{*} is defined by (3.31). Thus QMQ^{M} possesses a fixed point in EM∗E^{*}_{M} and its limit (u∞,v∞)(u^{\infty},v^{\infty}) as M→∞M\to\infty belongs to the set E∞∗E_{\infty}^{*} defined by the following constraints:

u0(x)≥0,v0(x)≥0,u0(x)+v0(x)≤K¯,∀x∈ℝ;u0(x)≤u¯∗(0,x),v0(x)≤u¯∗(0,x),∀x≥ξ0;supn∈ℕu¯∗(0,x+nL)≤u0(x),supn∈ℕv¯∗(0,x+nL)≤v0(x),∀x∈ℝ.\begin{array}[]{ll}u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ v_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x)\leq\overline{K},&{}^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R};\\[6.0pt] u_{0}(x)\leq\overline{u}^{*}(0,x),\quad\ v_{0}(x)\leq\overline{u}^{*}(0,x),&{}^{\forall}x\geq\xi_{0};\\[6.0pt] \displaystyle\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{u}^{*}(0,x+nL)\leq u_{0}(x),\ \ \sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\underline{v}^{*}(0,x+nL)\leq v_{0}(x),&{}^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{array}

As above, one easily sees that the vector function (u∞,v∞)(u^{\infty},v^{\infty}) satisfies (2.18) and (2.19), therefore it is the desired traveling wave. This completes the proof of Theorem 2.13. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.15.

The proof of the existence of right traveling waves for any super-critical speed c>cR∗=0c>c^{*}_{R}=0 is precisely the same as the proof of Theorem 2.13 for the case c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}, so we omit it. We now focus on the existence of a right stationary wave.

Let us explain how to adapt the argument in the proof of Theorem 2.13 for c=cR∗>0c=c^{*}_{R}>0 to the case where cR∗=0c^{*}_{R}=0. For τ>0\tau>0, we consider the solution map QτMQ^{M}_{\tau} defined by

QτM​(u0,v0)​(x)=(u⁡(τ,x),v⁡(τ,x)),Q^{M}_{\tau}(u_{0},v_{0})(x)=\left(u\left(\tau,x\right),v\left(\tau,x\right)\right), (3.32)

where (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) is the solution of the system (3.5) starting from the initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}). Let EM∗E^{*}_{M} be the set defined above. Since the subsolution (u¯∗,v¯∗)\big(\underline{u}^{*},\underline{v}^{*}\big) and the supersolution (u¯∗,v¯∗)\big(\overline{u}^{*},\overline{v}^{*}\big) are stationary, we have QτM​(EM∗)⊂EM∗Q^{M}_{\tau}(E^{*}_{M})\subset E^{*}_{M} for any τ>0\tau>0. As a consequence, there exists a fixed point (u0,τM​(x),v0,τM​(x))\big(u^{M}_{0,\tau}(x),v^{M}_{0,\tau}(x)\big), satisfying QτM​(u0,τM,v0,τM)​(x)=(u0,τM​(x),v0,τM​(x))Q^{M}_{\tau}\big(u^{M}_{0,\tau},v^{M}_{0,\tau}\big)(x)=\big(u^{M}_{0,\tau}(x),v^{M}_{0,\tau}(x)\big). The corresponding solution of (1.1), which we denote by (uτM​(t,x),vτM​(t,x))\big(u^{M}_{\tau}(t,x),v^{M}_{\tau}(t,x)\big), is therefore τ\tau-periodic in time. We consider the family of such solutions obtained by setting τ=2−k=:τk​(k∈ℕ)\tau=2^{-k}=:\tau_{k}\,(k\in\mathbb{N}). Since (u0,τkM​(x),v0,τkM​(x))=(uτkM​(1,x),vτkM​(1,x))\big(u^{M}_{0,\tau_{k}}(x),v^{M}_{0,\tau_{k}}(x)\big)=\big(u^{M}_{\tau_{k}}(1,x),v^{M}_{\tau_{k}}(1,x)\big), by the standard estimates on parabolic operators, the family {(u0,τkM,v0,τkM):k∈ℕ}\{\big(u^{M}_{0,\tau_{k}},v^{M}_{0,\tau_{k}}\big)\>:\>k\in\mathbb{N}\} is relatively compact with respect to the uniform topology; therefore, up to extracting a subsequence, it converges uniformly to a limit (u0,0M​(x),v0,0M​(x))\big(u^{M}_{0,0}(x),v^{M}_{0,0}(x)\big) as k→+∞k\to+\infty. Clearly (u0,0M​(x),v0,0M​(x))\big(u^{M}_{0,0}(x),v^{M}_{0,0}(x)\big) is time-periodic of period 2−k2^{-k} for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, therefore it is stationary. By taking the limit M→−∞M\to-\infty with the usual diagonal extraction procedure, we obtain a stationary wave for (1.1) that belongs to E∞∗E^{*}_{\infty}. This completes the proof of Theorem 2.15 ∎

3.3 Proof of uniqueness

Here we prove Theorem 2.19 on the uniqueness of traveling waves under the condition (2.24).

Proof of Theorem 2.19.

We just focus on right traveling waves, and deal with the case c≥cR∗>0c\geq c^{*}_{R}>0. The case c>cR∗=0c>c^{*}_{R}=0 follows from precisely the same arguments. By Proposition 2.2, the set

𝒯:={(u(x),v(x))∈BUC(ℝ)2:u(x)≥0,v(x)≥0 and u(x)+v(x)≤rmaxκmin}\mathcal{T}:=\left\{\big(u(x),v(x)\big)\in BUC(\mathbb{R})^{2}\>:\>u(x)\geq 0,v(x)\geq 0\text{ and }u(x)+v(x)\leq\frac{r_{\textrm{max}}}{\kappa_{\textrm{min}}}\right\} (3.33)

is positively invariant under the semiflow generated by (1.1). Furthermore, any nonnegative solution will eventually be attracted by 𝒯\mathcal{T}, uniformly in x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} as t→+∞t\to+\infty. Consequently, every traveling wave solution is contained in 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

We remark that, under the assumptions of the theorem, the system (1.1) is cooperative in 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Indeed, by (2.24), we have u+v≤μminκmaxu+v\leq\frac{\mu_{\min}}{\kappa_{\max}} in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, hence

∂fu∂v​(x,u,v)=μv​(x)−κu​(x)​u≥0,∂fv∂u​(x,u,v)=μu​(x)−κv​(x)​v≥0,\frac{\partial f_{u}}{\partial v}(x,u,v)=\mu_{v}(x)-\kappa_{u}(x)u\geq 0,\qquad\frac{\partial f_{v}}{\partial u}(x,u,v)=\mu_{u}(x)-\kappa_{v}(x)v\geq 0,

where fu​(x,u,v)f_{u}(x,u,v) and fv​(x,u,v)f_{v}(x,u,v) denote, respectively, the reaction terms in the first and the second line of (1.1). In particular, the classical comparison principle for cooperative parabolic systems holds true: given a subsolution (u¯​(t,x),v¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{u}(t,x),\underline{v}(t,x)\big) and a supersolution (u¯​(t,x),v¯​(t,x))\big(\overline{u}(t,x),\overline{v}(t,x)\big) satisfying 0≤u¯​(T,x)≤u¯​(T,x)0\leq\underline{u}(T,x)\leq\overline{u}(T,x), 0≤v¯​(T,x)≤v¯​(T,x)0\leq\underline{v}(T,x)\leq\overline{v}(T,x) for some T∈ℝT\in\mathbb{R} and for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, and (u¯​(t,⋅),v¯​(t,⋅))∈𝒯\big(\overline{u}(t,\cdot),\overline{v}(t,\cdot)\big)\in\mathcal{T} for all t≥Tt\geq T, we have

u¯(t,x)≤u¯(t,x), and v¯(t,x)≤v¯(t,x)∀t>T and ∀x∈ℝ.\underline{u}(t,x)\leq\overline{u}(t,x),\text{ and }\underline{v}(t,x)\leq\overline{v}(t,x)\qquad\,^{\forall}t>T\text{ and }\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}. (3.34)

Furthermore if u¯​(T,x)≢u¯​(T,x)\underline{u}(T,x)\not\equiv\overline{u}(T,x) or v¯​(T,x)≢v¯​(T,x)\underline{v}(T,x)\not\equiv\overline{v}(T,x), then the strict inequalities u¯​(t,x)<u¯​(t,x)\underline{u}(t,x)<\overline{u}(t,x) and v¯​(t,x)<v¯​(t,x)\underline{v}(t,x)<\overline{v}(t,x) holds for any t>Tt>T and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. By this remark and Theorem 2.17, the proof then follows from a classical sliding argument, which we recall here.

Let (u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big) and (u2​(t,x),v2​(t,x))\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big) be two traveling waves with speed c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R}. Since (1.1) is cooperative in 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the nonlinearity satisfies KPP-type conditions, it is classical that there exists a unique positive stationary solution (u∗​(x),v∗​(x))\big(u^{*}(x),v^{*}(x)\big) of (1.1). Furthermore, although our definition of traveling waves, Definition 6, only requires that the traveling wave be bounded below by a positive constant far behind the front, it is not difficult to show that any traveling wave in this broader sense converge to the positive steady state as x→−∞x\to-\infty, if the system is entirely cooperative. This follows by the shifting argument and the comparison principle. Thus we have

limx→−∞(|ui(t,x)−u∗(x)|+|vi(t,x)−v∗(x)|)=0,t∀∈ℝ,i=1,2.\lim_{x\to-\infty}\big(|u^{i}(t,x)-u^{*}(x)|+|v^{i}(t,x)-v^{*}(x)|\big)=0,\quad{}^{\forall}t\in\mathbb{R},\ i=1,2. (3.35)

See for example, [31, Theorem 2.1] or [21, Proposition 3.32]. We remark that (u1,γ​(t,x),v1,γ​(t,x)):=γ⁡(u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))\big(u^{1,\gamma}(t,x),v^{1,\gamma}(t,x)\big):=\gamma\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big) is a subsolution of (1.1) for all γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Fix t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} arbitrarily and x0≪−1x_{0}\ll-1. For x≤x0x\leq x_{0}, we have (u2​(t,x),v2​(t,x))≥1+γ2​(u∗​(x),v∗​(x))\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big)\geq\frac{1+\gamma}{2}\big(u^{*}(x),v^{*}(x)\big), and therefore there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that

(u2(t,x),v2(t,x))≥(u1,γ(t′,x)+ϵ,v1,γ(t′,x)+ϵ),∀t′∈ℝ and ∀x≤x0.\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big)\geq\big(u^{1,\gamma}(t^{\prime},x)+\epsilon,v^{1,\gamma}(t^{\prime},x)+\epsilon\big),\qquad^{\forall}t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }^{\forall}x\leq x_{0}. (3.36)

By Theorem 2.17 we know moreover that there exist constants α1,α2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0 such that

(u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))∼α1​eλ​(x−c​t)​(φλ​(x),ψλ​(x)), and (u2(t,x),v2(t,x))∼α2eλ(x−ct)(φλ(x),ψλ(x)), as x→+∞,\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big)\sim\alpha_{1}e_{\lambda}(x-ct)\big(\varphi^{\lambda}(x),\psi^{\lambda}(x)\big),\text{ and }\\ \big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big)\sim\alpha_{2}e_{\lambda}(x-ct)\big(\varphi^{\lambda}(x),\psi^{\lambda}(x)\big),\text{ as }x\to+\infty, (3.37)

where eλ​(ξ)=e−λ​ξe_{\lambda}(\xi)=e^{-\lambda\xi} if c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R} and eλ​(ξ)=ξ​e−λ∗​ξe_{\lambda}(\xi)=\xi e^{-\lambda^{*}\xi} if c=cRc=c_{R}. As a consequence, there exists t0t_{0} such that

(u2(t,x),v2(t,x))≥(u1,γ(t−t0,x),v1,γ(t−t0,x)),∀x∈ℝ.\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big)\geq\big(u^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{0},x),v^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{0},x)\big),\qquad^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}.

Define

t∗:=inf{t′∈ℝ:(u2(t,x),v2(t,x))≥(u1,γ(t−t′,x),v1,γ(t−t′,x)),∀x∈ℝ}.t_{*}:=\inf\{t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}\>:\>\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big)\geq\big(u^{1,\gamma}(t-t^{\prime},x),v^{1,\gamma}(t-t^{\prime},x)\big),\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}\}.

Then t∗≤t0<+∞t_{*}\leq t_{0}<+\infty. By the definition of t∗t_{*} we have u2​(t,x)≥u1,γ​(t−t∗,x)u^{2}(t,x)\geq u^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x) and v2​(t,x)≥v1,γ​(t−t∗,x)v^{2}(t,x)\geq v^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Moreover, u2u^{2} and u1,γu^{1,\gamma} are not identical because they have different behaviors as x→−∞x\to-\infty; therefore by the strong comparison principle we have the strict inequality

u2(t,x)=u2(t+L/c,x+L)>u1,γ(t−t∗+L/c,x+L)=u1,γ(t−t∗,x),∀x∈ℝ,u^{2}(t,x)=u^{2}(t+L/c,x+L)>u^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*}+L/c,x+L)=u^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x),\qquad^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R},

where we have used the pulsating relation (2.18); and similarly we conclude that v2​(t,x)>v1,γ​(t−t∗,x)v^{2}(t,x)>v^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. In view of this, (3.36) and the definition of t∗t_{*}, there exists a sequence xn→+∞x_{n}\to+\infty such that either limn→+∞u1,γ​(t−t∗,xn)u2​(t,xn)=1\lim_{n\to+\infty}\frac{u^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x_{n})}{u^{2}(t,x_{n})}=1, or limn→+∞v1,γ​(t−t∗,xn)v2​(t,xn)=1\lim_{n\to+\infty}\frac{v^{1,\gamma}(t-t_{*},x_{n})}{v^{2}(t,x_{n})}=1. In both cases, we obtain

1=limn→+∞γ​α1​eλ​(xn−c⁡(t−t∗))α2​eλ​(xn−c​t)=γ​α1α2​eλ​c​t∗,1=\lim_{n\to+\infty}\frac{\gamma\alpha_{1}e_{\lambda}\big(x_{n}-c(t-t_{*})\big)}{\alpha_{2}e_{\lambda}(x_{n}-ct)}=\gamma\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}}e^{\lambda ct_{*}},

so that

t∗=1λ​c​ln⁡(α2γ​α1).t_{*}=\frac{1}{\lambda c}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\gamma\alpha_{1}}\right).

By taking the limit γ→1\gamma\to 1 and up to redefining t∗t_{*}, we have shown the property that

(u1(t−t′,x),v1(t−t′,x))≤(u2(t,x),v2(t,x)),∀t′≥t∗:=1λ​cln(α2α1).\big(u^{1}(t-t^{\prime},x),v^{1}(t-t^{\prime},x)\big)\leq\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big),\qquad^{\forall}t^{\prime}\geq t_{*}:=\frac{1}{\lambda c}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}}\right). (3.38)

Exchanging the roles of (u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big) and (u2​(t,x),v2​(t,x))\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big) and arguing similarly, we obtain

(u1(t,x),v1(t,x))≥(u2(t−t′,x),v2(t−t′,x)),∀t′≥t∗′:=1λ​cln(α1α2)=−t∗.\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big)\geq\big(u^{2}(t-t^{\prime},x),v^{2}(t-t^{\prime},x)\big),\qquad^{\forall}t^{\prime}\geq t^{\prime}_{*}:=\frac{1}{\lambda c}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{2}}\right)=-t_{*}. (3.39)

This proves that (u1​(t−t∗,x),v1​(t−t∗,x))≡(u2​(t,x),v2​(t,x))\big(u^{1}(t-t_{*},x),v^{1}(t-t_{*},x)\big)\equiv\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big), for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, and consequently this equality holds for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. This proves uniqueness up to a time shift.

Now, we apply (3.38) to the pair (u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))=(u2​(t,x),v2​(t,x))\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big)=\big(u^{2}(t,x),v^{2}(t,x)\big). In this case α1=α2\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}, therefore we have t∗=0t_{*}=0. Hence (3.38) shows that (u1​(t,x),v1​(t,x))\big(u^{1}(t,x),v^{1}(t,x)\big) is time-increasing. This finishes the proof or Theorem 2.19. ∎

4 Exponential decay of traveling waves

In this section we focus on the exponential decay of traveling waves along the leading edge, as stated in Theorem 2.17. Throughout this section we fix c>0c>0. Our argument is largely inspired by the scalar case studied by Hamel [17]. As in [17], we make a change of variable to obtain compactness in the “space variable”, by introducing the following functions:

U⁡(t,x)=u⁡(t+xc,x);V⁡(t,x)=v⁡(t+xc,x).U(t,x)=u\left(\frac{t+x}{c},x\right);\ V(t,x)=v\left(\frac{t+x}{c},x\right). (4.1)

It is easily seen from the pulsating relation (2.18) that the new functions UU and VV are LL-periodic with respect to the xx variable and satisfy

c​Ut−σ⁡(x)​(Ut​t−2​Ut​x+Ux​x)+σx​(x)​(Ut−Ux)=fu​(x,U,V),c​Vt−σ⁡(x)​(Vt​t−2​Vt​x+Vx​x)+σx​(x)​(Vt−Vx)=fv​(x,U,V).\begin{split}cU_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(U_{tt}-2U_{tx}+U_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(U_{t}-U_{x}\big)&=f_{u}(x,U,V),\\ cV_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(V_{tt}-2V_{tx}+V_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(V_{t}-V_{x}\big)&=f_{v}(x,U,V).\end{split} (4.2)

Moreover, given U⁡(t,x)U(t,x) and V⁡(t,x)V(t,x), we can recover the original functions by the change of variables u⁡(t,x)=U⁡(c​t−x,x)u(t,x)=U\left(ct-x,x\right) and v⁡(t,x)=V⁡(c​t−x,x)v(t,x)=V\left(ct-x,x\right). With these functions U,VU,V, the statements (2.22), (2.23) of Theorem 2.17 are expressed in the following form:

limt→−∞U⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​φλ​(x)=limt→−∞V⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​ψλ​(x)=αuniformly inx∈ℝ,\lim_{t\to-\infty}\frac{U(t,x)}{e(t)\varphi^{\lambda}(x)}=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\frac{V(t,x)}{e(t)\psi^{\lambda}(x)}=\alpha\quad\hbox{uniformly in}\ \ x\in\mathbb{R}, (4.3)

where e⁡(t)=eλc​te(t)=e^{\lambda_{c}t} and λ=λc\lambda=\lambda_{c} if c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}, while e⁡(t)=−t​eλ∗​te(t)=-te^{\lambda^{*}t} and λ=λ∗\lambda=\lambda^{*} if c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}.

Let us give a brief summary of the structure of the proof. Although the system (4.2) is neither parabolic nor uniformly elliptic, the strong maximum principle still holds for (4.2), because the original equation is uniformly parabolic. Therefore, we can establish the sweeping principle (Proposition 4.1), which applies to a family of subsolutions (U¯μ,V¯μ)\big(\underline{U}_{\mu},\underline{V}_{\mu}\big) and supersolutions (U¯μ,V¯μ)\big(\overline{U}_{\mu},\overline{V}_{\mu}\big), to show that (U¯0,V¯0)≤(U¯0,V¯0)\big(\underline{U}_{0},\underline{V}_{0}\big)\leq\big(\overline{U}_{0},\overline{V}_{0}\big) implies (U¯1,V¯1)≤(U¯1,V¯1)\big(\underline{U}_{1},\underline{V}_{1}\big)\leq\big(\overline{U}_{1},\overline{V}_{1}\big). Then, we use this result to derive an analogue of the sliding method (Proposition 4.2). These two Propositions, along with the Harnack inequality derived in Lemma 4.3, constitute our main tools to establish the rate of decay along the leading edges of traveling waves.

Then, we start analyzing the exponential behavior of the leading edges of traveling waves. Proposition 4.4 is devoted to a rough exponential lower bound, while Proposition 4.5 establishes a rough exponential upper bound. The proofs are quite similar and rely on the same idea. For the lower bound, suppose by contradiction that there exists a sequence of points (tn,xn)(t_{n},x_{n}) with tn→−∞t_{n}\to-\infty such that (U⁡(tn),V⁡(tn))\big(U(t_{n}),V(t_{n})\big) converge to 0 faster than expected, i.e.

min⁡(U⁡(tn,xn),V⁡(tn,xn))≤Cn​eλ​tn,\min\big(U(t_{n},x_{n}),V(t_{n},x_{n})\big)\leq C_{n}e^{\lambda t_{n}},

where λ\lambda is the smallest positive solution of the equation λ​c=k⁡(λ)\lambda c=k(\lambda) (here we explain the argument for super-critical speeds, which is simpler). By using a supersolution of the type (U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x)):=eλ​t​(φλ​(x),ψλ​(x))\big(\overline{U}(t,x),\overline{V}(t,x)\big):=e^{\lambda t}\big(\varphi^{\lambda}(x),\psi^{\lambda}(x)\big) and the Harnack inequality, we can use the sliding method on the interval [tn,0][t_{n},0] to show that

min⁡(U⁡(0,xn),V⁡(0,xn))≤C~n,\min\big(U(0,x_{n}),V(0,x_{n})\big)\leq\tilde{C}_{n},

where C~n\tilde{C}_{n} converges to 00 as n→+∞n\to+\infty. Taking the limit, this is obviously a contradiction, since (U⁡(0,x),V⁡(0,x))\big(U(0,x),V(0,x)\big) are uniformly positive because of the periodicity. We proceed similarly for the upper bound. The technical details are slightly more involved for the critical case c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}. To summarize, we use a supersolution to derive a rough lower bound, and a subsolution to derive a rough upper bound, which may sound slightly unusual. As we shall see below, for a more refined lower bound, we use a family of subsolutions.

In Lemma 4.6, we prove the stronger property that

infx∈ℝmin⁡(U⁡(t,x)eλ​t​φλ​(x),V⁡(t,x)eλ​t​ψλ​(x))\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\min\left(\frac{U(t,x)}{e^{\lambda t}\varphi^{\lambda}(x)},\frac{V(t,x)}{e^{\lambda t}\psi^{\lambda}(x)}\right)

converges to a positive limit, say α\alpha, as t→−∞t\to-\infty. This is done by a family of subsolutions and the sweeping method (Proposition 4.1). To apply the sweeping method, we have to show that the starting member of the family of subsolutions lies below the traveling wave, which is guaranteed by the rough lower bound in Proposition 4.4. Again, the method is the same for the critical speed, but the computations are more involved. Note that, by shifting the time, we may assume without loss of generality that α=1\alpha=1 in the above limit.

Finally we prove (4.3) with α=1\alpha=1 by showing that

supx∈ℝmax⁡(U⁡(t,x)eλ​t​φλ​(x),V⁡(t,x)eλ​t​ψλ​(x))→1ast→−∞.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max\left(\frac{U(t,x)}{e^{\lambda t}\varphi^{\lambda}(x)},\frac{V(t,x)}{e^{\lambda t}\psi^{\lambda}(x)}\right)\to 1\quad\hbox{as}\ \ t\to-\infty.

This is done by a contradiction argument and the strong maximum principle.

The above strategy is, for the most part, similar to [17]. However, there are some important differences. Among other things, since the traveling wave does not necessarily lie in the cooperative region, we do not know if the traveling wave is increasing in tt entirely, which is in marked contrast with the scalar case. Another difficulty, which is also seen in the construction of the traveling wave in section 3, is that the two components of the subsolutions (U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{U}(t,x),\underline{V}(t,x)\big) do not necessarily become negative at the same position, therefore, we have to pay attention to the behavior of (U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{U}(t,x),\underline{V}(t,x)\big) even where they are negative.

We now proceed to the proof. We start with a comparison principle.

Proposition 4.1 (The sweeping method).

Let σ\sigma be a C1C^{1}, positive and LL-periodic function, and (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))\big(\overline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\overline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big) and (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))\big(\underline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\underline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big) be continuous with respect to μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], LL-periodic in xx and satisfy respectively

c​U¯t−σ⁡(x)​(U¯t​t−2​U¯t​x+U¯x​x)+σx​(x)​(U¯t−U¯x)≥gu​(x,U¯,V¯),c​V¯t−σ⁡(x)​(V¯t​t−2​V¯t​x+V¯x​x)+σx​(x)​(V¯t−V¯x)≥gv​(x,U¯,V¯),\begin{split}&c\overline{U}_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(\overline{U}_{tt}-2\overline{U}_{tx}+\overline{U}_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(\overline{U}_{t}-\overline{U}_{x}\big)\geq g_{u}(x,\overline{U},\overline{V}),\\ &c\overline{V}_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(\overline{V}_{tt}-2\overline{V}_{tx}+\overline{V}_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(\overline{V}_{t}-\overline{V}_{x}\big)\geq g_{v}(x,\overline{U},\overline{V}),\end{split} (4.4)

and

c​U¯t−σ⁡(x)​(U¯t​t−2​U¯t​x+U¯x​x)+σx​(x)​(U¯t−U¯x)≤gu​(x,U¯,V¯),c​V¯t−σ⁡(x)​(V¯t​t−2​V¯t​x+V¯x​x)+σx​(x)​(V¯t−V¯x)≤gv​(x,U¯,V¯),\begin{split}&c\underline{U}_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(\underline{U}_{tt}-2\underline{U}_{tx}+\underline{U}_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(\underline{U}_{t}-\underline{U}_{x}\big)\leq g_{u}(x,\underline{U},\underline{V}),\\ &c\underline{V}_{t}-\sigma(x)\big(\underline{V}_{tt}-2\underline{V}_{tx}+\underline{V}_{xx}\big)+\sigma_{x}(x)\big(\underline{V}_{t}-\underline{V}_{x}\big)\leq g_{v}(x,\underline{U},\underline{V}),\end{split} (4.5)

in the classical sense, for all μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], t∈[T1,T2]t\in[T_{1},T_{2}] and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, where g=(gu,gv)g=(g_{u},g_{v}) is a cooperative nonlinearity that is also locally Lipschitz in (U,V)(U,V) and LL-periodic in xx. Suppose that the following three statements hold true.

U¯μ(T1,x)<U¯μ(T1,x),V¯μ(T1,x)<V¯μ(T1,x),∀x∈ℝ and ∀μ∈[0,1),\underline{U}_{\mu}(T_{1},x)<\overline{U}_{\mu}(T_{1},x),\quad\underline{V}_{\mu}(T_{1},x)<\overline{V}_{\mu}(T_{1},x),\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }\,^{\forall}\mu\in[0,1), (4.6a)
U¯μ(T2,x)<U¯μ(T2,x),V¯μ(T2,x)<V¯μ(T2,x),∀x∈ℝ and ∀μ∈[0,1),\underline{U}_{\mu}(T_{2},x)<\overline{U}_{\mu}(T_{2},x),\quad\underline{V}_{\mu}(T_{2},x)<\overline{V}_{\mu}(T_{2},x),\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }\,^{\forall}\mu\in[0,1), (4.6b)
U¯0(t,x)≤U¯0(t,x),V¯0(t,x)≤V¯0(t,x),∀(t,x)∈[T1,T2]×ℝ.\underline{U}_{0}(t,x)\leq\overline{U}_{0}(t,x),\quad\underline{V}_{0}(t,x)\leq\overline{V}_{0}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}. (4.6c)

Then,

U¯1​(t,x)≤U¯1​(t,x)​ and ​V¯1​(t,x)≤V¯1​(t,x), for all ​(t,x)∈[T1,T2]×ℝ.\underline{U}_{1}(t,x)\leq\overline{U}_{1}(t,x)\text{ and }\underline{V}_{1}(t,x)\leq\overline{V}_{1}(t,x),\text{ for all }(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}. (4.7)

If U¯μ>0\overline{U}_{\mu}>0 and V¯μ>0\overline{V}_{\mu}>0 for all μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1), then the inequalities (4.5) need to be satisfied only on the set of (μ,t,x)(\mu,t,x) where either U¯μ​(t,x)>0\underline{U}_{\mu}(t,x)>0 or V¯μ​(t,x)>0\underline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)>0.

Proof.

Let us define

μ∗:=sup{μ≥0:U¯μ(t,x)≤U¯μ(t,x) and V¯μ(t,x)≤V¯μ(t,x),∀(t,x)∈[T1,T2]}.\mu^{*}:=\sup\{\mu\geq 0\>:\>\underline{U}_{\mu}(t,x)\leq\overline{U}_{\mu}(t,x)\text{ and }\underline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\leq\overline{V}_{\mu}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2}]\}. (4.8)

Then there exists a sequence of points (μn,tn,xn)∈(μ∗,1]×[T1,T2]×ℝ(\mu_{n},t_{n},x_{n})\in(\mu^{*},1]\times[T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R} with μn→μ∗\mu_{n}\to\mu^{*} as n→+∞n\to+\infty, such that

 either U¯μn(tn,xn)>U¯μn(tn,xn) or V¯μn(tn,xn)>V¯μn(tn,xn),∀n∈ℕ.\text{ either }\underline{U}_{\mu_{n}}(t_{n},x_{n})>\overline{U}_{\mu_{n}}(t_{n},x_{n})\text{ or }\underline{V}_{\mu_{n}}(t_{n},x_{n})>\overline{V}_{\mu_{n}}(t_{n},x_{n}),\qquad\,^{\forall}n\in\mathbb{N}. (4.9)

Then (u¯,v¯)(\overline{u},\overline{v}) and (u¯,v¯)(\underline{u},\underline{v}) satisfy

u¯t−(σ⁡(x)​u¯x)x\displaystyle\overline{u}_{t}-\big(\sigma(x)\overline{u}_{x}\big)_{x} ≥gu​(x,u¯,v¯),\displaystyle\geq g_{u}(x,\overline{u},\overline{v}), (4.11)
v¯t−(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x\displaystyle\overline{v}_{t}-\big(\sigma(x)\overline{v}_{x}\big)_{x} ≥gv​(x,u¯,v¯),\displaystyle\geq g_{v}(x,\overline{u},\overline{v}),

and

v¯t−(σ⁡(x)​v¯x)x\displaystyle\underline{v}_{t}-\big(\sigma(x)\underline{v}_{x}\big)_{x} ≤gv​(x,u¯,v¯).\displaystyle\leq g_{v}(x,\underline{u},\underline{v}).

A direct consequence of Proposition 4.1 is the following result, known as the “sliding method”.

Proposition 4.2 (The sliding method).

Let Assumption 1 hold true, and (U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\overline{U}(t,x),\overline{V}(t,x)\big) and (U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{U}(t,x),\underline{V}(t,x)\big) be LL-periodic in xx and satisfy respectively (4.4) and (4.5) in the classical sense, for all t∈[T1,T2]t\in[T_{1},T_{2}] and x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, where g=(gu,gv)g=(g_{u},g_{v}) is cooperative nonlinearity that is also locally Lipschitz in (U,V)(U,V) and LL-periodic in xx. Suppose that:

  1. 1.

    Either

    U¯(T1,x)<U¯(t,x),V¯(T1,x)<V¯(t,x),∀(t,x)∈(T1,T2]×ℝ,\underline{U}(T_{1},x)<\overline{U}(t,x),\quad\underline{V}(T_{1},x)<\overline{V}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in(T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}, (4.14a)
    and
    U¯(T2,x)>U¯(t,x),V¯(T2,x)>V¯(t,x),∀(t,x)∈[T1,T2)×ℝ;\overline{U}(T_{2},x)>\underline{U}(t,x),\quad\overline{V}(T_{2},x)>\underline{V}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2})\times\mathbb{R}; (4.14b)
  2. 2.

    Or,

    U¯(T2,x)<U¯(t,x),V¯(T2,x)<V¯(t,x),∀(t,x)∈[T1,T2)×ℝ,\underline{U}(T_{2},x)<\overline{U}(t,x),\quad\underline{V}(T_{2},x)<\overline{V}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2})\times\mathbb{R}, (4.15a)
    and
    U¯(T1,x)>U¯(t,x),V¯(T1,x)>V¯(t,x),∀(t,x)∈(T1,T2]×ℝ;\overline{U}(T_{1},x)>\underline{U}(t,x),\quad\overline{V}(T_{1},x)>\underline{V}(t,x),\,^{\forall}(t,x)\in(T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}; (4.15b)

Then

U¯​(t,x)≥U¯​(t,x)​ and ​V¯​(t,x)≥V¯​(t,x), for all ​(t,x)∈[T1,T2]×ℝ.\overline{U}(t,x)\geq\underline{U}(t,x)\text{ and }\overline{V}(t,x)\geq\underline{V}(t,x),\text{ for all }(t,x)\in[T_{1},T_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}. (4.16)
Proof.

To prove assertion 11, we apply the sweeping method (Proposition 4.1) to the family of sub- and supersolutions defined by (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))=(U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\underline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\underline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big)=\big(\underline{U}(t,x),\underline{V}(t,x)\big) and (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))=(U¯​(t+(1−μ)​(T2−T1),x),V¯​(t+(1−μ)​(T2−T1),x))\big(\overline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\overline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big)=\big(\overline{U}(t+(1-\mu)(T_{2}-T_{1}),x),\overline{V}(t+(1-\mu)(T_{2}-T_{1}),x)\big).

The proof of assertion 22 is similar to that of assertion 11, by using the family (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))=(U¯​(t+(1−μ)​(T2−T1),x),V¯​(t+(1−μ)​(T2−T1),x))\big(\underline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\underline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big)=\big(\underline{U}(t+(1-\mu)(T_{2}-T_{1}),x),\underline{V}(t+(1-\mu)(T_{2}-T_{1}),x)\big) and (U¯μ​(t,x),V¯μ​(t,x))=(U¯​(t,x),V¯​(t,x))\big(\overline{U}_{\mu}(t,x),\overline{V}_{\mu}(t,x)\big)=\big(\overline{U}(t,x),\overline{V}(t,x)\big). ∎

Lemma 4.3 (Harnack-type estimate).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} be fixed. There exists a constant H>0H>0 such that for any classical solution (U⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x))\big(U(t,x),V(t,x)\big) of (4.2) with (t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}, one has

min⁡(U⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x))≥H−1​max⁡(U⁡(t,y),V⁡(t,y))\min\big(U(t,x),V(t,x)\big)\geq H^{-1}\max\big(U(t,y),V(t,y)\big) (4.17)

for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and all (x,y)∈ℝ×ℝ(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

We come back to the original variables by setting u⁡(t,x)=U⁡(c​t−x,x)u(t,x)=U(ct-x,x) and v⁡(t,x)=V⁡(c​t−x,x)v(t,x)=V(ct-x,x); then (u,v)(u,v) is an entire solution of the parabolic system (1.1). In order to obtain (4.17), it is sufficient to establish that

infs∈[t/c,(t+L)/c]x∈[−2​L,L]​min⁡(u⁡(s,x),v⁡(s,x))≥H−1​sups∈[(t−2​L)/c,(t−L)/c]x∈[−2​L,L]​max⁡(u⁡(s,x),v⁡(s,x)).\underset{x\in[-2L,L]}{\inf_{s\in[t/c,(t+L)/c]}}\min\big(u(s,x),v(s,x)\big)\geq H^{-1}\underset{x\in[-2L,L]}{\sup_{s\in[(t-2L)/c,(t-L)/c]}}\max\big(u(s,x),v(s,x)\big). (4.18)

The Harnack inequality established by Földes and Poláčik [9, Theorem 3.9] provides a constant κ\kappa depending only on θ\theta such that for any τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R},

infs∈[τ+7/2​θ,τ+4​θ]x∈[−2​L,L]​min⁡(u⁡(s,x),v⁡(s,x))≥κ​sups∈[τ+θ,τ+2​θ]x∈[−2​L,L]​max⁡(u⁡(s,x),v⁡(s,x)).\underset{x\in[-2L,L]}{\inf_{s\in[\tau+7/2\theta,\tau+4\theta]}}\min\big(u(s,x),v(s,x)\big)\geq\kappa\underset{x\in[-2L,L]}{\sup_{s\in[\tau+\theta,\tau+2\theta]}}\max\big(u(s,x),v(s,x)\big). (4.19)

Selecting θ=L/c\theta=L/c and τ=(t−3​L)/c\tau=(t-3L)/c we obtain (4.18) with H=1κH=\frac{1}{\kappa} and therefore (4.17). ∎

We can now obtain a lower bound of the leading edge of the traveling wave.

Proposition 4.4 (Lower rough bound of the leading edge).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} be fixed. Let (U⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x))\big(U(t,x),V(t,x)\big) be a classical, nonnegative and nontrivial solution of (4.2). Then,

where C~n:=2​H​max⁡(φλc,ψλc)min⁡(φλc,ψλc)​Cn\widetilde{C}_{n}:=2H\frac{\max(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}})}{\min(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}})}C_{n}. It follows from elementary computations that the vector function

satisfies (4.4) with gu​(x,u,v)=u⁡(ru​(x)−μu​(x))+μv​(x)​vg_{u}(x,u,v)=u\big(r_{u}(x)-\mu_{u}(x)\big)+\mu_{v}(x)v and gv​(x,u,v)=v⁡(rv​(x)−μv​(x))+μu​(x)​ug_{v}(x,u,v)=v\big(r_{v}(x)-\mu_{v}(x)\big)+\mu_{u}(x)u (there is even equality), and (U⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x))\big(U(t,x),V(t,x)\big) satisfies (4.5) with the same gg, which is cooperative. Next we prove (4.21). We follow the same steps. Assume by contradiction that (4.21) does not hold, then there exist sequences tn→−∞t_{n}\to-\infty, xn∈ℝx_{n}\in\mathbb{R} and Cn→0C_{n}\to 0 such that

Proposition 4.5 (Upper rough bound of the leading edge).

Let Assumption 1 hold true and let c≥cR∗c\geq c^{*}_{R} be fixed. Let (U⁡(t,x),V⁡(t,x))\big(U(t,x),V(t,x)\big) be a classical, nonnegative and nontrivial solution of (4.2), that vanishes when t→+∞t\to+\infty. Then,

    if c>cR∗c>c^{*}_{R}, there is a constant C>0C>0 and T∈ℝT\in\mathbb{R} such that

    U(t,x)≤Ceλc​tφλc(x) and V(t,x)≤Ceλc​tψλc(x),∀t≤T,∀x∈ℝ,U(t,x)\leq Ce^{\lambda_{c}t}\varphi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)\text{ and }V(t,x)\leq Ce^{\lambda_{c}t}\psi^{\lambda_{c}}(x),\qquad\,^{\forall}t\leq T,\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}, (4.27)

    where λc>0\lambda_{c}>0 is the smallest positive solution of λc​c=k⁡(λc)\lambda_{c}c=k(\lambda_{c});

  2. 2.

    if c=cR∗c=c^{*}_{R}, there is a constant C>0C>0 and T∈ℝT\in\mathbb{R} such that

    U(t,x)≤C|t|eλ∗​tφλ∗(x) and V(t,x)≤C|t|eλ∗​tψλ∗(x),∀t≤T,∀x∈ℝ,U(t,x)\leq C|t|e^{\lambda^{*}t}\varphi^{\lambda^{*}}(x)\text{ and }V(t,x)\leq C|t|e^{\lambda^{*}t}\psi^{\lambda^{*}}(x),\qquad\,^{\forall}t\leq T,\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}, (4.28)

    where λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 is the smallest positive solution of λ∗​c=k⁡(λ∗)\lambda^{*}c=k(\lambda^{*}).

Proof.

Let us prove (4.27) first. Assume by contradiction that (4.27) does not hold, then there exist sequences tn→−∞t_{n}\to-\infty, xn∈ℝx_{n}\in\mathbb{R} and Cn→+∞C_{n}\to+\infty such that

U⁡(tn,xn)≥Cn​eλc​tn​φλc​(xn)​ or ​V​(tn,xn)≥Cn​eλc​tn​ψλc​(xn).U(t_{n},x_{n})\geq C_{n}e^{\lambda_{c}t_{n}}\varphi^{\lambda_{c}}(x_{n})\text{ or }V(t_{n},x_{n})\geq C_{n}e^{\lambda_{c}t_{n}}\psi^{\lambda_{c}}(x_{n}).

By the Harnack inequality (4.17) in Lemma 4.3 we deduce

U(tn,x)>C~neλc​tnφλc(x) and V(tn,x)>C~neλc​tnψλc(x),∀x∈ℝ,U(t_{n},x)>\widetilde{C}_{n}e^{\lambda_{c}t_{n}}\varphi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)\text{ and }V(t_{n},x)>\widetilde{C}_{n}e^{\lambda_{c}t_{n}}\psi^{\lambda_{c}}(x),\qquad\,^{\forall}x\in\mathbb{R}, (4.29)

where C~n:=12​H​min⁡(φλc,ψλc)max⁡(φλc,ψλc)​Cn\widetilde{C}_{n}:=\frac{1}{2H}\frac{\min(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}})}{\max(\varphi^{\lambda_{c}},\psi^{\lambda_{c}})}C_{n}. Let (u¯ω​(t,x),v¯ω​(t,x))\big(\underline{u}_{\omega}(t,x),\underline{v}_{\omega}(t,x)\big) be defined by (3.11) with ω≥ω∗\omega\geq\omega^{*} so that the differential inequality (3.12) is satisfied by applying Lemma 3.4 (β\beta is chosen sufficiently large so that the system (3.2) is cooperative). Define

In other words,

U¯ω​(t,x)=eλc​t​φλc​(x)−ω​eν​t​φν​(x)​ and ​V¯ω​(t,x)=eλc​t​ψλc​(x)−ω​eν​t​ψν​(x),\underline{U}_{\omega}(t,x)=e^{\lambda_{c}t}\varphi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)-\omega e^{\nu t}\varphi^{\nu}(x)\text{ and }\underline{V}_{\omega}(t,x)=e^{\lambda_{c}t}\psi^{\lambda_{c}}(x)-\omega e^{\nu t}\psi^{\nu}(x),

Changing the variable in (3.12), we obtain that (U¯ω,V¯ω)(\underline{U}_{\omega},\underline{V}_{\omega}) satisfies the differential inequality (4.5) for any t≤−ξωt\leq-\xi_{\omega}, with

+u~∞​(ru−μu)+μv​ψφ​v~∞\displaystyle\quad+\tilde{u}_{\infty}\big(r_{u}-\mu_{u}\big)+\mu_{v}\frac{\psi}{\varphi}\tilde{v}_{\infty}
=∂x(σ​∂xu~∞)+2​σ​(−λ+φ′φ)​∂xu~∞+u~∞​[k⁡(λ)−λ​c]⏟=0+μv​ψφ​(v~∞−u~∞),\displaystyle=\partial_{x}(\sigma\partial_{x}\tilde{u}_{\infty})+2\sigma\left(-\lambda+\frac{\varphi^{\prime}}{\varphi}\right)\partial_{x}\tilde{u}_{\infty}+\tilde{u}_{\infty}\underset{=0}{\underbrace{\big[k(\lambda)-\lambda c\big]}}+\mu_{v}\frac{\psi}{\varphi}(\tilde{v}_{\infty}-\tilde{u}_{\infty}), (4.47a)

and moreover (up to further extraction) xn→x∞∈[0,L]x_{n}\to x_{\infty}\in[0,L]. Because of (4.44) we have (u~∞,v~∞)≥(1,1)\big(\tilde{u}_{\infty},\tilde{v}_{\infty}\big)\geq(1,1) and for each t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} there exists x0​(t)∈ℝx_{0}(t)\in\mathbb{R} such that either

limt→−∞infx∈ℝmin⁡(U⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​φλ​(x),V⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​ψλ​(x))=limt→−∞supx∈ℝmax⁡(U⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​φλ​(x),V⁡(t,x)e⁡(t)​ψλ​(x))=1.\lim_{t\to-\infty}\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\min\left(\frac{U(t,x)}{e(t)\varphi^{\lambda}(x)},\frac{V(t,x)}{e(t)\psi^{\lambda}(x)}\right)=\lim_{t\to-\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max\left(\frac{U(t,x)}{e(t)\varphi^{\lambda}(x)},\frac{V(t,x)}{e(t)\psi^{\lambda}(x)}\right)=1.

This establishes the claim (4.3) with α=1\alpha=1, and the proof of Theorem 2.17 is complete. ∎

5 Behavior behind the front

In this section, we study the behavior of traveling waves far behind the front, under the assumption that the coefficients are spatially homogeneous, for that the spatial period LL is very small (the rapidly oscillating case). A large part of the arguments here rely on the results we presented in our previous paper [15].

5.1 The homogeneous case

In this subsection we assume that the coefficients of (1.1) are spatially homogeneous. We begin with the existence of a unique homogeneous equilibrium for (1.1).

Lemma 5.1 (Existence and uniqueness of stationary state [15]).

Let ru,rv∈ℝr_{u},r_{v}\in\mathbb{R}, κu>0\kappa_{u}>0, κv>0\kappa_{v}>0, and μu,μv>0\mu_{u},\mu_{v}>0. Assume that λA>0\lambda_{A}>0, where λA\lambda_{A} denotes the principal eigenvalue of the matrix AA in (2.26). Then, there exists a unique positive homogeneous steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) for (1.1).

Proof.

The proof follows from algebraic computations on the system satisfied by the homogeneous steady state. We refer to [15, Lemma 12] for the details. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.20.

It is shown in Theorem 2.4 of our previous paper [15] that any nonnegative solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) to the Cauchy problem for (2.25) with nontrivial initial data converges to (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) in the sense that, for each 0<c<cR∗(=cL∗)0<c<c^{*}_{R}\,(=c^{*}_{L}), it holds that

limt→+∞sup|x|≤c​tmax⁡(|u⁡(t,x)−u∗|,|v⁡(t,x)−v∗|)=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{|x|\leq ct}\max\big(|u(t,x)-u^{*}|,|v(t,x)-v^{*}|\big)=0.

Hence

limt→+∞max⁡(|u⁡(t,0)−u∗|,|v⁡(t,0)−v∗|)=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\max\big(|u(t,0)-u^{*}|,|v(t,0)-v^{*}|\big)=0. (5.1)

In particular, if (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) is a right traveling wave of the form (U⁡(x−c​t),V⁡(x−c​t))\big(U(x-ct),V(x-ct)\big), then it is easily seen that (5.1) is equivalent to (2.28). Similarly, if (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) is a left traveling wave of the form (U⁡(x+c​t),V⁡(x+c​t))\big(U(x+ct),V(x+ct)\big), (5.1) is equivalent to

limξ→+∞(U⁡(ξ),V⁡(ξ))=(u∗,v∗).\lim_{\xi\to+\infty}\big(U(\xi),V(\xi)\big)=(u^{*},v^{*}).

This completes the proof of Theorem 2.20. ∎

5.2 The rapidly oscillating case

Next, we deal with the case where the spatial period L=εL=\varepsilon is sufficiently small. We begin with the following lemma, which is an analog of Lemma 5.1 in the previous subsection.

Lemma 5.2 (Existence and uniqueness of rapidly oscillating entire solution [15]).

Let the assumptions of Theorem 2.21 hold. Then there exists ε¯\bar{\varepsilon} such that for any 0<ε≤ε¯0<\varepsilon\leq\bar{\varepsilon}, the system (2.29) possesses a unique entire solution (uε∗,vε∗)(u^{*}_{\varepsilon},v^{*}_{\varepsilon}) that is bounded from above and from below by positive constants, and this entire solution is an ε\varepsilon-periodic stationary solution.

Proof.

The proof of this result has been given in our former paper [15, Lemma 21]. ∎

Now we are ready to prove assertion 2 of Theorem 2.21

Proof of Theorem 2.21.

The claim (2.33) is proved in Lemma 18 of our previous paper [15]. By Theorem 2.5 of [15], any nonnegative solution (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))\big(u(t,x),v(t,x)\big) to the Cauchy problem for (2.29) with nontrivial initial data satisfies, for any c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} with 0<c1<cε,L∗0<c_{1}<c^{*}_{\varepsilon,L}, 0<c2<cε,R∗0<c_{2}<c^{*}_{\varepsilon,R},

limt→+∞sup−c1​t≤x≤c2​t(|u⁡(t,x)−uε∗​(x)|+|v⁡(t,x)−vε∗​(x)|)=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{-c_{1}t\leq x\leq c_{2}t}\big(|u(t,x)-u^{*}_{\varepsilon}(x)|+|v(t,x)-v^{*}_{\varepsilon}(x)|\big)=0.

Hence

limt→+∞sup0≤x≤ε(|u(t,x)−uε∗(x)+|v(t,x)−vε∗(x)|)=0.\lim_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{0\leq x\leq\varepsilon}\big(|u(t,x)-u^{*}_{\varepsilon}(x)+|v(t,x)-v^{*}_{\varepsilon}(x)|\big)=0. (5.2)

In particular, if (u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),v(t,x)) is a right traveling wave, then by the condition (2.18),

u(t+εc,x)=u(t,x−ε),v(t+εc,x)=v(t,x−ε),for all(t,x)∈ℝ2,u\left(t+\frac{\varepsilon}{c},x\right)=u(t,x-\varepsilon),\;v\left(t+\frac{\varepsilon}{c},x\right)=v(t,x-\varepsilon),\ \ \text{for all}\ \ (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

therefore, it is not difficult to see that (5.2) implies (2.34). Left traveling waves can be treated similarly by using (2.20). This completes the proof of Theorem 2.21. ∎

6.2 Analysis of the limit problem

Uniform derivative estimates

Let us study the limit problem of (EPλ) with (2.36) as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0. As before, we impose

Let us first show that φ,φ′,ψ,ψ′\varphi,\varphi^{\prime},\psi,\psi^{\prime} are uniformly bounded on [δ,L][\delta,L] as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0. The uniform boundedness of φ\varphi is already shown in (6.13). In order to prove the uniform boundedness of φ′\varphi^{\prime}, we prepare the following lemma.

Lemma 6.1.

Let Φ\Phi be a C2C^{2} function on an interval [a,b][a,b] satisfying the equation

Φ′′​(z)=F⁡(z)(a<z<b).\Phi^{\prime\prime}(z)=F(z)\quad(a<z<b). (6.17)

Then the following estimates hold:

|Φ⁡(z)|≤max⁡(|Φ⁡(a)|,|Φ⁡(b)|)+(b−z)​(z−a)b−a​∫ab|Φ⁡(ξ)|​dξ,|Φ′​(z)|≤|Φ⁡(b)−Φ⁡(a)|b−a+∫ab|Φ⁡(ξ)|​dξ.\begin{split}&|\Phi(z)|\leq\max\left(|\Phi(a)|,|\Phi(b)|\right)+\frac{(b-z)(z-a)}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b}|\Phi(\xi)|\mathrm{d}\xi,\\ &|\Phi^{\prime}(z)|\leq\frac{\left|\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)\right|}{b-a}+\int_{a}^{b}|\Phi(\xi)|\mathrm{d}\xi.\end{split} (6.18)
Proof.

The solution of the equation (6.17) is given in the following form

Φ⁡(z)=(b−z)​Φ​(a)+(z−a)​Φ​(b)b−a+∫abG⁡(z,ξ)​F​(ξ)​𝑑ξ.\Phi(z)=\frac{(b-z)\Phi(a)+(z-a)\Phi(b)}{b-a}+\int_{a}^{b}G(z,\xi)F(\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi.

where G⁡(z,ξ)G(z,\xi) denotes the Green’s function on the interval [a,b][a,b], namely

G⁡(z,ξ)={−(ξ−a)​(b−z)b−a(if​z≥ξ)−(z−a)​(b−ξ)b−a(if​z<ξ)G(z,\xi)=\begin{cases}\,-\dfrac{(\xi-a)(b-z)}{b-a}&(\hbox{if}\ z\geq\xi)\\[6.0pt] \,-\dfrac{(z-a)(b-\xi)}{b-a}&(\hbox{if}\ z<\xi)\end{cases}

The estimates (6.18) follow easily from the above expression, so we omit the details. ∎

Now let us prove the uniform boundedness of φ′\varphi^{\prime}. Since e−λ​z​φ​(z)e^{-\lambda z}\varphi(z) satisfies the equation (6.12), we see from the above lemma that e−λ​z​φ​(z)e^{-\lambda z}\varphi(z) and (e−λ​z​φ​(z))′\left(e^{-\lambda z}\varphi(z)\right)^{\prime} are uniformly bounded. Consequently φ′\varphi^{\prime} is uniformly bounded on [0,δ][0,\delta] as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0.

Next we prove the uniform boundedness of ψ\psi, ψ′\psi^{\prime}. Note that ψ\psi satisfies the second line of (6.8) on δ<z<L\delta<z<L, which we can rewrite as

(e−λ​z​ψ)′′=(k−r)​(e−λ​z​ψ)(δ<z<L).\left(e^{-\lambda z}\psi\right)^{\prime\prime}=(k-r)\left(e^{-\lambda z}\psi\right)\quad(\delta<z<L). (6.19)

If k≥rk\geq r, then (e−λ​z​ψ)\left(e^{-\lambda z}\psi\right) is convex. This, together with (6.14) and (6.15), implies that ψ\psi is uniformly bounded. Arguing as we did for φ\varphi, we obtain the uniform boundedness of ψ′\psi^{\prime}.

Next, if k<rk<r, by summing up the two equations in (EPλ) and integrating over [0,L][0,L], we obtain

(k−λ2−1)​∫0Lφ⁡(z)​dz=(λ2+r−k)​∫0Lψ⁡(z)​dz.Hence(r−λ2−1)​∫0Lφ⁡(z)​dz>λ2​∫0Lψ⁡(z)​dz.\begin{split}&(k-\lambda^{2}-1)\int_{0}^{L}\varphi(z)\mathrm{d}z=(\lambda^{2}+r-k)\int_{0}^{L}\psi(z)\mathrm{d}z.\\ &\ \ \hbox{Hence}\ \ \ (r-\lambda^{2}-1)\int_{0}^{L}\varphi(z)\mathrm{d}z>\lambda^{2}\int_{0}^{L}\psi(z)\mathrm{d}z.\end{split}

Since the left-hand side of the above inequality is uniformly bounded as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0, so is the right-hand side. In particular, ∫δLψ⁡(z)​𝑑z\int_{\delta}^{L}\psi(z)\mathrm{d}z is uniformly bounded as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0. Combining this with (6.14), (6.15), and applying Lemma 6.1, we see that ψ,ψ′\psi,\psi^{\prime} are uniformly bounded on [δ,L][\delta,L] as ε.δ→0\varepsilon.\delta\to 0.

Formulation of the limit problem

Now we let ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0 while keeping ε=O⁡(δ2)\varepsilon=O(\delta^{2}). The interval [0,δ][0,\delta] shrinks to the point z=0z=0. Since φ,φ′,ψ,ψ′\varphi,\varphi^{\prime},\psi,\psi^{\prime} are uniformly bounded as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0, we see, by the bootstrap argument for (6.8) that φ′′,φ′′′,ψ′′,ψ′′′\varphi^{\prime\prime},\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime},\psi^{\prime\prime},\psi^{\prime\prime\prime} are also uniformly bounded on [δ,L][\delta,L] as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0. Note also that, by (6.2), the eigenvalue k⁡(λ,ε,δ)k(\lambda;\varepsilon,\delta) varies within the range

λ2+1<k⁡(λ,ε,δ)<λ2+r.\lambda^{2}+1<k(\lambda;\varepsilon,\delta)<\lambda^{2}+r.

Consequently, for any sequence εn,δn→0\varepsilon_{n},\delta_{n}\to 0 with εn=O⁡(δn2)\varepsilon_{n}=O(\delta_{n}^{2}), we can extract a subsequence (εnj,δnj)(\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}) such that (φ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj),ψ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj))(\varphi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}),\psi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}})) converges to some function (φ0​(z,λ),ψ0​(z,λ))(\varphi_{0}(z;\lambda),\psi_{0}(z;\lambda)) on (0,L](0,L] as j→∞j\to\infty in the C2C^{2} sense and k(λ,,εnj,δnj)k(\lambda,,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}) to some constant k0k_{0} as j→∞j\to\infty. Needless to say, since (φ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj),ψ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj))(\varphi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}),\psi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}})) are LL-periodic, so is the limit (φ0,ψ0)(\varphi_{0},\psi_{0}), but this function has discontinuity at z=0z=0. In view of (6.10), (6.11), (6.15), (6.14) and (6.16), we see that (φ0,ψ0,k0)(\varphi_{0},\psi_{0},k_{0}) is a solution of the following limit problem:

{φ′′−2​λ​φ′+(λ2+1)​φ=k​φ(0<z<L),φ(+0)=1+μ,φ(L−0)=1,φ⁡(z)>0(0<z<L),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\,\varphi^{\prime\prime}-2\lambda\varphi^{\prime}+(\lambda^{2}+1)\varphi=k\varphi\ \ \ (0<z<L),\\[2.0pt] \,\varphi(+0)=1+\mu,\ \ \varphi(L-0)=1,\\[2.0pt] \,\varphi(z)>0\ \ \ (0<z<L),\end{cases} (6.20a)
{ψ′′−2​λ​ψ′+(λ2+r)​ψ=k​ψ(0<z<L),ψ(+0)=1,ψ(L−0)=1+μ,ψ⁡(z)>0(0<z<L),\displaystyle\begin{cases}\,\psi^{\prime\prime}-2\lambda\psi^{\prime}+(\lambda^{2}+r)\psi=k\psi\ \ \ (0<z<L),\\[2.0pt] \psi(+0)=1,\ \ \psi(L-0)=1+\mu,\\[2.0pt] \,\psi(z)>0\ \ \ (0<z<L),\end{cases} (6.20b)
φ′​(+0)+ψ′​(+0)=φ′​(L−0)+ψ′​(L−0).\displaystyle\varphi^{\prime}(+0)+\psi^{\prime}(+0)=\varphi^{\prime}(L-0)+\psi^{\prime}(L-0). (6.20c)

Note that (6.20a) and (6.20b) are separate boundary value problems for φ\varphi and ψ\psi, and they are coupled only through the condition (6.20c), which plays a crucial role. More precisely, for each kk in a certain range, one can solve (6.20a) and (6.20b) separately, but the resulting pair (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) satisfies the condition (6.20c) only for a special value of kk. In this sense, (6.20) can be regarded as an eigenvalue problem with kk being the eigenvalue. The following theorem holds:

Theorem 6.2 (The limit eigenproblem).

For each λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, there is a unique value of kk, denoted by k0​(λ)k_{0}(\lambda), for which (6.20) has a solution (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi). Furthermore, the principal eigenvalue k⁡(λ,ε,δ)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta) of (EPλ) with (2.36) converges to k0​(λ)k_{0}(\lambda) as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0 locally uniformly in λ\lambda, provided that ε=O⁡(δ2)\varepsilon=O(\delta^{2}).

Before proving the above theorem, let us make some preliminary analysis. By summing up the equations in (6.20a) and (6.20b) and integrating over 0<z<L0<z<L and using (6.20c), we obtain

(k0−λ2−1)​∫0Lφ0​(z)​𝑑z=(λ2+r−k0)​∫0Lψ0​(z)​𝑑z.(k_{0}-\lambda^{2}-1)\int_{0}^{L}\varphi_{0}(z)\mathrm{d}z=(\lambda^{2}+r-k_{0})\int_{0}^{L}\psi_{0}(z)\mathrm{d}z.

Since the two integrals are both positive and since r>1r>1, we have

λ2+1<k0<λ2+r(λ∀∈ℝ).\lambda^{2}+1<k_{0}<\lambda^{2}+r\quad({}^{\forall}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}). (6.21)

Thus we can retrieve the inequality (6.2) directly from the limit problem (6.20).

Now we fix λ\lambda arbitrarily, and let kk be a positive constant that is not necessarily the eigenvalue of (6.20). The equations (6.20a), (6.20b) can be rewritten as follows:

(e−λ​zφ)′′=(k−1)(e−λ​zφ),(e−λ​zψ)′′=(k−r)(e−λ​zψ)(0<z<L).\left(e^{-\lambda z}\varphi\right)^{\prime\prime}=(k-1)\left(e^{-\lambda z}\varphi\right),\ \ \ \left(e^{-\lambda z}\psi\right)^{\prime\prime}=(k-r)\left(e^{-\lambda z}\psi\right)\quad(0<z<L).

Therefore, in order for (6.20a) and (6.20b) to have positive solutions, both k−1k-1 and k−rk-r have to be larger than the principal eigenvalue ν\nu of the following problem, namely −π2/L2-\pi^{2}/L^{2} :

Φ′′=ν​Φ​(0<z<L),Φ⁡(0)=Φ⁡(L)=0.\Phi^{\prime\prime}=\nu\hskip 1.0pt\Phi\ (0<z<L),\quad\ \Phi(0)=\Phi(L)=0.

Hence

k>r−π2L2.k>r-\frac{\pi^{2}}{L^{2}}. (6.22)

Conversely, for any kk satisfying (6.22), the boundary value problems (6.20a), (6.20b) have unique solutions, which we denote by (φ⁡(z,k),ψ⁡(z,k))\big(\varphi(z;k),\psi(z;k)\big). Define

f⁡(k)=φ′​(L−0,k)−φ′​(+0,k),g⁡(k)=ψ′​(L−0,k)−ψ′​(+0,k)f(k)=\varphi^{\prime}(L-0;k)-\varphi^{\prime}(+0;k),\quad g(k)=\psi^{\prime}(L-0;k)-\psi^{\prime}(+0,k)

and

F⁡(k)=f⁡(k)+g⁡(k)=φ′​(L−0,k)+ψ′​(L−0,k)−φ′​(+0,k)−ψ′​(+0,k).F(k)=f(k)+g(k)=\varphi^{\prime}(L-0;k)+\psi^{\prime}(L-0;k)-\varphi^{\prime}(+0;k)-\psi^{\prime}(+0,k). (6.23)

Then (6.20c) holds if and only if F⁡(k)=0F(k)=0.

Proof of Theorem 6.2.

Fix λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} arbitrarily. Since we already know the existence of a solution of (6.20) as a limit of the sequence (φ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj),ψ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj))(\varphi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}),\psi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}})) and k⁡(λ,εnj,δnj)k(\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}), let us prove the uniqueness of the solution. It suffices to show that F⁡(k)F(k) is strictly monotone in kk.

Choose arbitrary constants k~>k\tilde{k}>k satisfying (6.22) and let

φ⁡(z):=φ⁡(z,k),φ~​(z):=φ⁡(z,k~),ψ⁡(z):=ψ⁡(z,k),ψ~​(z):=ψ⁡(z,k~).\varphi(z):=\varphi(z;k),\ \ \widetilde{\varphi}(z):=\varphi(z,\tilde{k}),\ \ \psi(z):=\psi(z;k),\ \ \widetilde{\psi}(z):=\psi(z;\tilde{k}).

Then

φ′′−2​λ​φ′+(λ2+1)​φ=k​φ,φ~′′−2​λ​φ~′+(λ2+1)​φ~=k~​φ~≥k​φ~.\varphi^{\prime\prime}-2\lambda\varphi^{\prime}+(\lambda^{2}+1)\varphi=k\varphi,\quad\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime\prime}-2\lambda\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime}+(\lambda^{2}+1)\widetilde{\varphi}=\tilde{k}\widetilde{\varphi}\geq k\widetilde{\varphi}.

Therefore φ~\widetilde{\varphi} is a subsolution of the equation satisfied by φ\varphi, and φ~​(+0)=φ​(+0)\widetilde{\varphi}(+0)=\varphi(+0), φ~​(L−0)=φ​(L−0)\widetilde{\varphi}(L-0)=\varphi(L-0). The function w=φ~−φw=\widetilde{\varphi}-\varphi then satisfies

(e−λ​z​w)′′≥(k−1)​(e−λ​z​w)(0<z<L),w⁡(+0)=w⁡(L−0)=0.\left(e^{-\lambda z}w\right)^{\prime\prime}\geq(k-1)\left(e^{-\lambda z}w\right)\ \ (0<z<L),\quad w(+0)=w(L-0)=0.

Since k−1>−π2/L2k-1>-\pi^{2}/L^{2} by (6.22), we can apply the strong maximum principle to show that w​(z)<0​(0<z<L)w(z)<0\;(0<z<L) and that w′​(+0)<0w^{\prime}(+0)<0, w′​(L−0)>0w^{\prime}(L-0)>0. In other words,

φ~​(z)<φ⁡(z)(0<z<L),φ~′​(+0)<φ′​(+0),φ~′​(L−0)>φ′​(L−0).\widetilde{\varphi}(z)<\varphi(z)\ \ (0<z<L),\quad\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime}(+0)<\varphi^{\prime}(+0),\quad\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime}(L-0)>\varphi^{\prime}(L-0).

Hence

f⁡(k~)−f⁡(k)=φ~′​(L−0)−φ~′​(+0)−(φ′​(L−0)−φ′​(+0))>0.f(\tilde{k})-f(k)=\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime}(L-0)-\widetilde{\varphi}^{\prime}(+0)-\left(\varphi^{\prime}(L-0)-\varphi^{\prime}(+0)\right)>0.

This implies that f⁡(k)f(k) is strictly monotone increasing. Similarly, g⁡(k)g(k) is strictly monotone increasing, therefore F⁡(k)F(k) is strictly monotone increasing in the range r−π2/L2<k<∞r-\pi^{2}/L^{2}<k<\infty. This proves the uniqueness of the solution of (6.20) for each given λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}.

Since any sequence of solutions (φ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj),ψ⁡(z,λ,εnj,δnj)),k⁡(λ,εnj,δnj)(\varphi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}),\psi(z,\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}})),k(\lambda,\varepsilon_{n_{j}},\delta_{n_{j}}) of (EPλ) has a subsequence that converges to a solution of (6.20) and since the solution of (6.20) is unique, we see that the solution (φ⁡(z,λ,ε,δ),ψ⁡(z,λ,ε,δ))(\varphi(z;\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta),\psi(z;\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)\big) of (EPλ) with (2.36) converges to the unique solution of the problem (6.20) as ε,δ→0\varepsilon,\delta\to 0 without taking a subsequence, and that k⁡(λ,ε,δ)→k0​(λ)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)\to k_{0}(\lambda). Furthermore, since k⁡(λ,ε,δ)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta) is convex in λ\lambda, the convergence k(λ,ε,δ)→k0(λ)(ε,δ→0)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)\to k_{0}(\lambda)\;(\varepsilon,\delta\to 0) is locally uniform in λ\lambda, since a pointwise convergence of a sequence of convex functions is uniform on bounded sets ([25, Theorem 10.8]). This completes the proof of Theorem 6.2. ∎

Comparison in the limit problem

Lemma 6.3.

Let k0​(λ)k_{0}(\lambda) be as in Theorem 6.2. Then

k0​(λ)​<k0​(−λ)for allλ>​0.k_{0}(\lambda)<k_{0}(-\lambda)\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ \lambda>0. (6.24)
Proof.

For each λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and kk satisfying (6.22), let φ⁡(z,k,λ),ψ⁡(z,k,λ)\varphi(z;k,\lambda),\psi(z;k,\lambda) denote the solution of (6.20a), (6.20b), and define

f⁡(k,λ)=φ′​(L−0,k,λ)−φ′​(+0,k,λ),g⁡(k,λ)=ψ′​(L−0,k,λ)−ψ′​(+0,k,λ),f(k;\lambda)=\varphi^{\prime}(L-0;k,\lambda)-\varphi^{\prime}(+0;k,\lambda),\quad g(k;\lambda)=\psi^{\prime}(L-0;k,\lambda)-\psi^{\prime}(+0;k,\lambda),
F⁡(k,λ)=f⁡(k,λ)+g⁡(k,λ).F(k;\lambda)=f(k;\lambda)+g(k;\lambda).

As we have seen above, F⁡(k,λ)F(k;\lambda) is strictly increasing in kk, and F⁡(k,λ)=0F(k;\lambda)=0 if and only if k=k0​(λ)k=k_{0}(\lambda). In order to make a finer estimate of k0​(λ)k_{0}(\lambda), we compute f⁡(k,λ)f(k;\lambda) and g⁡(k,λ)g(k;\lambda) explicitly.

We start with f⁡(k,λ)f(k;\lambda). The characteristic equation for (6.20a) is given by

X2−2​λ​X+λ2+1−k=0.X^{2}-2\lambda X+\lambda^{2}+1-k=0.

In view of (6.21), it suffices to consider kk in the range λ2+1<k<λ2+r\lambda^{2}+1<k<\lambda^{2}+r. In particular, we may assume k>1k>1, hence the solution of the above characteristic equation is given by

X±=λ±k−1.X^{\pm}=\lambda\pm\sqrt{k-1}.

Thus the solution of (6.20a) is written in the form

φ⁡(z,k,λ)=C+​eX+​z+C−​eX−​z,\varphi(z;k,\lambda)=C^{+}e^{X^{+}z}+C^{-}e^{X^{-}z},

with C+,C−C^{+},C^{-} being determined by the boundary conditions φ⁡(+0)=1+μ\varphi(+0)=1+\mu, φ⁡(L−0)=1\varphi(L-0)=1. A simple calculation then shows the following, where α=k−1\alpha=\sqrt{k-1}:

f⁡(k,λ)=−μ​λ+αeα​L−e−α​L​((μ+2)​(eα​L+e−α​L)−2​((1+μ)​eλ​L+e−λ​L)).f(k;\lambda)=-\mu\lambda+\frac{\alpha}{e^{\alpha L}-e^{-\alpha L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\alpha L}+e^{-\alpha L}\right)-2\left((1+\mu)e^{\lambda L}+e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right). (6.25)

Next we consider g⁡(k,λ)g(k;\lambda). The solution of (6.20b) can be expressed by using the roots of Y2−2​λ​Y+λ2+r−k=0Y^{2}-2\lambda Y+\lambda^{2}+r-k=0, but the expression differs depending on the sign of k−rk-r.

(a) The case k>rk>r: In this case, the roots of the characteristic equation are real, so g⁡(k,λ)g(k;\lambda) can be computed in the same manner as above, and we have the following, where β=k−r\beta=\sqrt{k-r}:

g⁡(k,λ)=μ​λ+βeβ​L−e−β​L​((μ+2)​(eβ​L+e−β​L)−2​(eλ​L+(1+μ)​e−λ​L)).g(k;\lambda)=\mu\lambda+\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta L}-e^{-\beta L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\beta L}+e^{-\beta L}\right)-2\left(e^{\lambda L}+(1+\mu)e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right). (6.26)

(b) The case k=rk=r: This case is the limit of the above case as k→rk\to r (or β→0\beta\to 0), thus

g⁡(k,λ)=μ​λ+1L​(μ+2−(eλ​L+(1+μ)​e−λ​L)).g(k;\lambda)=\mu\lambda+\frac{1}{L}\left(\mu+2-\left(e^{\lambda L}+(1+\mu)e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right). (6.27)

(c) The case k<rk<r: In this case, we also need use (6.22) which is a necessary condition for the existence of a positive solution of (6.20b). The solution ψ\psi is expressed by a linear combination of eλ​z​cos⁡ω​ze^{\lambda z}\cos\omega z and eλ​z​sin⁡ω​ze^{\lambda z}\sin\omega z, where ω=r−k\omega=\sqrt{r-k}, and we get

g⁡(k,λ)=λ​μ+ωsin⁡ω​L​((μ+2)​cos⁡ω​L−(eλ​L+(1+μ)​e−λ​L)).g(k;\lambda)=\lambda\mu+\frac{\omega}{\sin\omega L}\left((\mu+2)\cos\omega L-\left(e^{\lambda L}+(1+\mu)e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right). (6.28)

Note that the expression of g⁡(k,λ)g(k;\lambda) in (6.28) can also be obtained by replacing β\beta in (6.26) by i​ωi\omega. So these two expressions are identical.

Now we assume λ>0\lambda>0, and compare F⁡(k,λ):=f⁡(k,λ)+g⁡(k,λ)F(k;\lambda):=f(k;\lambda)+g(k;\lambda) and F⁡(k,−λ):=f⁡(k,−λ)+g⁡(k,−λ)F(k;-\lambda):=f(k;-\lambda)+g(k;-\lambda). In the case where k>rk>r, (6.25) and (6.27) give

F⁡(k,λ)=αeα​L−e−α​L​((μ+2)​(eα​L+e−α​L)−2​((1+μ)​eλ​L+e−λ​L))+βeβ​L−e−β​L​((μ+2)​(eβ​L+e−β​L)−2​(eλ​L+(1+μ)​e−λ​L)),\begin{split}F(k,\lambda)&=\frac{\alpha}{e^{\alpha L}-e^{-\alpha L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\alpha L}+e^{-\alpha L}\right)-2\left((1+\mu)e^{\lambda L}+e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right)\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta L}-e^{-\beta L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\beta L}+e^{-\beta L}\right)-2\left(e^{\lambda L}+(1+\mu)e^{-\lambda L}\right)\right),\end{split}
F⁡(k,−λ)=αeα​L−e−α​L​((μ+2)​(eα​L+e−α​L)−2​((1+μ)​e−λ​L+eλ​L))+βeβ​L−e−β​L​((μ+2)​(eβ​L+e−β​L)−2​(e−λ​L+(1+μ)​eλ​L)).\begin{split}F(k,-\lambda)&=\frac{\alpha}{e^{\alpha L}-e^{-\alpha L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\alpha L}+e^{-\alpha L}\right)-2\left((1+\mu)e^{-\lambda L}+e^{\lambda L}\right)\right)\\ &\hskip 20.0pt+\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta L}-e^{-\beta L}}\left((\mu+2)\left(e^{\beta L}+e^{-\beta L}\right)-2\left(e^{-\lambda L}+(1+\mu)e^{\lambda L}\right)\right).\end{split}

Consequently,

F⁡(k,λ)−F⁡(k,−λ)=2​μ​(eλ​L−e−λ​L)​(βeβ​L−e−β​L−αeα​L−e−α​L).F(k;\lambda)-F(k;-\lambda)=2\mu\left(e^{\lambda L}-e^{-\lambda L}\right)\left(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta L}-e^{-\beta L}}-\frac{\alpha}{e^{\alpha L}-e^{-\alpha L}}\right).

Since λ>0\lambda>0, α>β\alpha>\beta, and since y/(ey​L−e−y​L)y/(e^{yL}-e^{-yL}) is monotone decreasing in yy, we have

F⁡(k,λ)>F⁡(k,−λ)for​λ>0F(k;\lambda)>F(k;-\lambda)\quad\hbox{for}\ \lambda>0 (6.29)

if k>rk>r. The same inequality also holds for the range r≥k>r−π2/L2r\geq k>r-\pi^{2}/L^{2}, as one can easily see by using (6.27) and (6.28). The details are omitted.

Recall that both F⁡(k,λ)F(k;\lambda) and F⁡(k,−λ)F(k;-\lambda) are strictly increasing in kk, and that F⁡(k0​(λ),λ)=F⁡(k0​(−λ),−λ)=0F(k_{0}(\lambda),\lambda)=F(k_{0}(-\lambda),-\lambda)=0. In view of this and (6.29), we obtain (6.24). The lemma is proved. ∎

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 2.22.

Proof of Theorem 2.22.

Recall that we have, by (6.1),

cR∗​(ε,δ)=minλ>0⁡k⁡(λ,ε,δ)λ,cL∗​(ε,δ)=minλ>0⁡k⁡(−λ,ε,δ)λ,c^{*}_{R}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\min_{\lambda>0}\frac{k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)}{\lambda},\quad c^{*}_{L}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\min_{\lambda>0}\frac{k(-\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)}{\lambda}, (6.30)

where k⁡(λ,ε,δ)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta) denotes the principal eigenvalue of (EPλ) with (2.36). Furthermore, as shown in (6.3), the minima in (6.30) are attained by λ\lambda that lies in the following range:

r−r−1≤λ≤r+r−1.\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1}\leq\lambda\leq\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r-1}.

By Theorem 6.2, the convergence k(λ,ε,δ)→k0(λ)(ε,δ→0)k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)\to k_{0}(\lambda)\;(\varepsilon,\delta\to 0) is locally uniform in λ\lambda. This, together with (6.24), implies that

k⁡(λ,ε,δ)<k⁡(−λ,ε,δ)for​λ∈[r−r−1,r+r−1]k(\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)<k(-\lambda,\varepsilon,\delta)\quad\hbox{for}\ \,\lambda\in[\sqrt{r}-\sqrt{r-1},\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{r-1}]

for all sufficiently small ε,δ\varepsilon,\delta with ε=O⁡(δ2)\varepsilon=O(\delta^{2}), hence (2.37). This establishes Theorem 2.22. ∎
